definitions.definition: For the purposes of section 203, 'breath test' means a test for the purpose of obtaining an indication of the presence of alcohol in a person's blood carried out, on one or more specimens of breath provided by that person, by means of a device of a type approved by the Central Government, by notification in the Official Gazette, for the purpose of such a test.
definitions.plain_english: A breath test is a roadside or on-site test where a driver blows into an approved device that checks whether there is alcohol in their blood. A police officer in uniform or an authorised Motor Vehicles Department officer can ask any driver in a public place to take this test if they have reasonable suspicion of drunk driving. The device used must be officially approved by the Central Government and listed in the Official Gazette.
real_world_examples: A traffic police officer in Mumbai stops a car driver at a late-night nakabandi (checkpoint) on the Western Express Highway and asks the driver to blow into an Alcoblow breathalyser to check for alcohol consumption before allowing him to proceed.

Following a road accident near Connaught Place in Delhi involving two vehicles, a uniformed police officer suspects the driver of the offending car had been drinking and requires him to provide a breath specimen on the spot using a Central Government-approved breath analyser device.

A police officer in Bengaluru notices a two-wheeler rider swerving erratically on MG Road at night and pulls him over, requiring him to undergo a breath test at the nearest police post using an officially approved device to determine if alcohol is present in his blood.

During a special enforcement drive in Chennai ahead of a festival, Motor Vehicles Department officers authorised for the purpose set up checkpoints and administer breath tests to multiple drivers using approved devices to detect drunk driving before it causes accidents.

A truck driver involved in a fatal accident on the NH-44 near Nagpur is required by an on-duty police officer to provide a breath specimen at the accident site; the positive reading on the approved device leads to his arrest without warrant under section 203.
what_it_covers: A test carried out using one or more breath specimens provided by a driver, using a Central Government-notified approved device, to indicate the presence of alcohol in the blood.

Breath tests administered at or near the location where the requirement is made in a public place, including at a police station or at a hospital (in accident cases), by a uniformed police officer or an authorised Motor Vehicles Department officer.
Breath tests conducted on a person who has been arrested and brought to a police station, where they must be given an opportunity to provide a breath specimen.
Tests whose results are admissible as evidence in legal proceedings related to offences under section 185 of the Motor Vehicles Act.
what_it_excludes: Blood specimen analysis conducted at a laboratory, which falls under 'laboratory test' as defined in section 204 and is a separate and distinct procedure.

Any test carried out using a device not approved and notified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette, as such a device-based test would not qualify as a valid breath test under this definition.

Breath tests administered on a person who is an indoor patient at a hospital if the registered medical practitioner in immediate charge of the patient's case has not been notified or objects on medical grounds.

Urine tests, saliva tests, or any other physiological specimen-based tests for detecting alcohol or drugs, which are not covered by the definition of 'breath test'.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a valid breath test has been conducted determines whether a police officer has lawful grounds to arrest a driver without a warrant under section 203, and whether the test result can be admitted as evidence in a prosecution for the offence of driving under the influence of alcohol under section 185. A refusal or failure to submit to a breath test can itself be treated as a circumstance supporting the prosecution's case under section 205, making the definition critical to both enforcement and evidentiary outcomes.

definitions.definition: A canvasser is a person who engages in soliciting custom for public service vehicles, including the sale of tickets for travel by such vehicles, and who is required under Section 93 of the Motor Vehicles Act to obtain a licence from the prescribed authority subject to conditions laid down by the State Government.
definitions.plain_english: A canvasser is someone who actively goes out to attract passengers or sell travel tickets on behalf of buses, minibuses, or other public transport vehicles. Think of them as a promoter or tout who drums up business for a transport operator. They must hold a valid government-issued licence to do this job legally, and they cannot advertise their services without displaying their licence details.
real_world_examples: A person standing outside Kashmere Gate ISBT in Delhi loudly calling out destinations and persuading travellers to board a particular private bus to Chandigarh — this person is acting as a canvasser and must hold a valid State Government licence.

An agent at a small-town bus stand in Tamil Nadu selling reserved seats or tickets for a private stage carriage service to Chennai on behalf of the operator, without being the driver or conductor, is functioning as a licensed canvasser.

A tout near a Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation bus stand who approaches incoming passengers and diverts them to a private tempo traveller service by soliciting business is operating as a canvasser and requires a licence under Section 93.

A booking office employee in Rajasthan who works independently (not directly employed by the transport company) to collect passengers and issue tickets for a contract carriage service plying between Jaipur and Ajmer must be licensed as a canvasser.

An online ticketing aggregator agent physically present at a Hyderabad bus terminal who redirects passengers to specific private bus operators in exchange for commission is performing canvassing activities covered under this provision.
what_it_covers: Any individual who solicits passengers at bus stands, railway stations, or public places on behalf of a public service vehicle operator.
A person who sells or arranges tickets for travel on stage carriages, contract carriages, or other public service vehicles as an independent intermediary.
An agent who advertises travel services on behalf of a public service vehicle operator in newspapers, directories, or other publications and thereby solicits custom.
A person who physically intercepts or approaches travellers to redirect them to a specific transport service in exchange for a commission or fee.
what_it_excludes: Drivers and conductors of public service vehicles who are directly employed by the operator and hold separate licences under the Act — they are not canvassers.
Agents exclusively engaged in collecting, forwarding, or distributing goods carried by goods carriages, who fall under a separate category under Section 93(1)(b) and are not classified as canvassers.

Employees of state transport undertakings (e.g., KSRTC, MSRTC) who sell tickets at official counters as part of their employment — they act within an institutional framework and are not independent canvassers.
Online travel platforms or apps operating purely digitally without any physical solicitation of passengers at transport hubs, as the canvasser role involves direct personal solicitation of custom.
definitions.why_it_matters: A person acting as a canvasser without obtaining the mandatory licence under Section 93 commits an offence under the Motor Vehicles Act, exposing them to penalties including suspension or forfeiture of security deposit. The definition is critical because it determines whether an individual must obtain a State Government licence, comply with advertising disclosure conditions, and deposit security — obligations that directly affect their legal right to operate in the transport solicitation space.

definitions.definition: A cause of action, as used in Section 155 of the Motor Vehicles Act, refers to the legal right to institute proceedings arising out of an event that has given rise to a claim under the provisions relating to insurance against third-party risks, which survives the death of the claimant and may be enforced against the deceased's estate or against the insurer.
definitions.plain_english: A 'cause of action' is the legal basis or right that allows a person to file a claim for compensation after a motor accident. Under Section 155, even if the injured person dies after the accident, their right to claim compensation does not die with them — it can still be pursued by their legal heirs against the responsible party's insurance company or the deceased's estate. In simple terms, the accident itself creates the right to sue, and that right survives death.
real_world_examples: A pedestrian is seriously injured in a road accident in Delhi involving an insured vehicle. The pedestrian files a compensation claim before the Claims Tribunal but dies of natural causes two months later while the case is pending. Under Section 155, the cause of action survives and his legal heirs can continue the claim against the insurer.

A passenger in a private car is injured in an accident on the Mumbai-Pune Expressway. She suffers grievous injuries and initiates a legal claim. She passes away a week later due to unrelated cardiac arrest. Her family can still proceed with the original compensation claim arising from the accident, as the cause of action does not extinguish.

A motorcyclist in Bengaluru is hit by a goods vehicle. He sustains permanent disability, engages a pleader, and files a claim before the Claims Tribunal. He dies before the award is passed due to old age. His legal representatives can continue the case because the cause of action — the accident — had already arisen before his death.

A farmer in rural Maharashtra is knocked down by a bus and suffers bodily injury. He obtains a certificate of insurance detail and prepares to file a claim. He dies one month after the accident before formally filing the case. His family can still file and pursue the claim because the cause of action arose at the time of the accident.

In a hit and run motor accident in Chennai, the victim survives long enough to register a complaint with the police and file a claim. He subsequently succumbs to his injuries. The cause of action having already arisen upon the happening of the accident, his estate and insurer remain liable, and his heirs may proceed to enforce the claim.
what_it_covers: Any right to claim compensation that arises from a motor accident event covered under the insurance provisions of the Act, where the claimant dies after the event but before the claim is resolved.
Claims against the insurer of the vehicle involved in the accident, which survive the death of the certificate of insurance holder or injured person.
Causes of action that accrue to the injured person's estate and can be pursued by legal representatives even if the original claimant is no longer alive.
Situations where death occurs after the accident event but during the pendency of proceedings before the Claims Tribunal.
Cases where the certificate of insurance had been issued before the accident and the death of the insured occurs post-accident.
what_it_excludes: A cause of action where the person dies before the accident event occurs — no right to claim arises posthumously in the first place.
Claims based on events that do not fall under the insurance provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act, such as pure contractual disputes or criminal proceedings unrelated to the accident.
The creation of a new or extended cause of action after death — Section 155 only preserves an existing cause of action that had already arisen; it does not create fresh rights.
Causes of action under unrelated statutes or contracts that happen to involve deceased persons, which are governed by their own survivorship rules.
Claims where no certificate of insurance had been issued in favour of the deceased — absence of insurance coverage takes the claim outside the scope of this provision.
definitions.why_it_matters: Section 155 directly determines whether a compensation claim under the Motor Vehicles Act survives the death of the claimant — if this definition applies, the insurer and the estate remain liable and legal heirs can enforce the claim; if it does not apply, the claim may be extinguished under general succession law principles found in Section 306 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925. It thus controls whether the insurer's obligation to pay compensation is triggered or discharged upon the claimant's death.

definitions.definition: The Central Government means the Government of India, as constituted under the Constitution of India, exercising executive authority at the national level. Though not expressly defined in Section 2 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, it refers to the Union Government acting through the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, empowered under this Act to issue notifications, make rules, and exercise regulatory functions of a national character.
definitions.plain_english: The Central Government means the Government of India, based in New Delhi, which runs the country at the national level. In the context of the Motor Vehicles Act, it is the Union Government — typically the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways — that has the power to make rules, issue notifications, and set standards that apply across all states. It is different from a State Government, which only governs within its own state.
real_world_examples: The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (Central Government) issues a notification in the Official Gazette appointing the date on which the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 comes into force in a particular State.

The Central Government exercises its power under Section 18 of the MV Act to frame rules related to the grant of driving licences for motor vehicles used in connection with Central Government undertakings such as defence establishments.

Under Section 26 of the MV Act, the Central Government prescribes the form and conditions governing the maintenance of registers of driving licences, ensuring uniformity across all licensing authorities in India.

The Union Cabinet, acting as the Central Government, approves an amendment to the Motor Vehicles Act and directs that new emission standards and vehicle safety norms be notified under the Act with nationwide applicability.

The Central Government, through its designated Ministry, enters into reciprocal arrangements with foreign countries under the MV Act to recognise driving licences issued by those countries for use in India.
what_it_covers: The Government of India acting through the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways when exercising powers under the MV Act.
Any officer, authority, or body to whom the Central Government has delegated its functions under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988.
The Union Cabinet and its ministries when issuing notifications, framing rules, or appointing dates of commencement under the Act.
Central Government departments or undertakings such as defence or railways operating motor vehicles, in respect of whom the Central Government may exercise special regulatory authority.
The President of India acting on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers, as the constitutional basis of Central Government executive action under the Act.
what_it_excludes: State Governments of individual states such as Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, or Uttar Pradesh, which have separate regulatory authority under the Act within their respective territories.
Local authorities such as municipal corporations or panchayats, which are not considered the Central Government even when performing transport-related functions.
Autonomous bodies, statutory corporations, or transport undertakings (e.g., KSRTC, DTC) that are not direct arms of the Central Government executive.
Courts, tribunals, or quasi-judicial bodies established under the MV Act, which exercise judicial rather than executive governmental functions.
Regional Transport Authorities or State Transport Authorities, which are creatures of State Government and do not constitute the Central Government.
definitions.why_it_matters: The distinction between Central Government and State Government is critical under the MV Act because certain rule-making powers, licensing conditions, and notifications — particularly under Sections 18 and 26 — vest exclusively in the Central Government, and any action taken without proper Central Government authority would be ultra vires and legally invalid. Rules framed or notifications issued by the Central Government have nationwide binding effect, triggering compliance obligations on all licensing authorities, registering authorities, and transport operators across India.

definitions.definition: A certificate of fitness is a document issued by the prescribed authority or an authorised testing station, in the form and containing the particulars prescribed by the Central Government, certifying that a transport vehicle complies for the time being with all the requirements of the Motor Vehicles Act and the rules made thereunder, and without which a transport vehicle shall not be deemed to be validly registered for the purposes of section 39.
definitions.plain_english: A certificate of fitness is an official document that confirms a commercial or transport vehicle (like a bus, truck, or taxi) is in a safe and roadworthy condition and meets all legal standards set by the government. It is issued by a government-appointed authority or an approved vehicle testing station after a physical inspection of the vehicle. Without this certificate, a transport vehicle cannot legally operate on Indian roads, even if it has a valid registration.
real_world_examples: A bus operator in Maharashtra running a state-route bus service must obtain a certificate of fitness from the Regional Transport Office (RTO) every year, confirming that the bus's brakes, lights, tyres, and body structure meet prescribed safety standards before it can carry passengers.

A goods truck owner in Punjab applies to the authorised testing station at the district transport office to get his vehicle inspected; after the vehicle passes the inspection for load-bearing capacity, emission norms, and braking systems, a certificate of fitness is issued allowing the truck to legally transport goods.

definitions.definition: A certificate issued by an authorised insurer in pursuance of sub-section (3) of section 147, and includes a cover note complying with such requirements as may be prescribed, and where more than one certificate has been issued in connection with a policy, or where a copy of a certificate has been issued, all those certificates or that copy, as the case may be.
definitions.plain_english: A certificate of insurance is an official document issued by a licensed insurance company to the vehicle owner, confirming that the motor vehicle is covered by a valid insurance policy as required by law. It serves as proof that the vehicle is insured against third-party liabilities such as injury or property damage. A cover note issued before the formal certificate is also treated as a certificate of insurance if it meets the prescribed requirements.
real_world_examples: A truck driver in Maharashtra is stopped at a police checkpost; the traffic officer demands the certificate of insurance, and the driver produces the document issued by New India Assurance Company confirming third-party liability cover for the goods carriage.

A two-wheeler owner in Delhi purchases a new bike and, while the formal certificate is being processed, receives a cover note from HDFC ERGO as a temporary certificate of insurance, which is accepted at an RTO registration check.

An autorickshaw owner in Chennai is asked by the Regional Transport Authority to produce the certificate of insurance alongside the fitness certificate during a transport vehicle inspection; she submits a duly attested photocopy within the prescribed 15-day period.

After a road accident in Bengaluru involving a private car, the Claims Tribunal requires the owner to produce the certificate of insurance issued by Bajaj Allianz to verify third-party coverage before processing the compensation claim of the injured pedestrian.

A bus operator in Uttar Pradesh obtains insurance from a government insurance fund and receives two certificates — one for the primary policy and one for an additional endorsement — and both are treated together as the certificate of insurance under the Act.

A traffic police officer in Hyderabad intercepts a vehicle under Section 206 and demands the certificate of insurance; the owner, unable to produce it immediately, is required to submit it within the prescribed period to avoid penalty.
what_it_covers: A formal certificate issued by an authorised insurer under Section 147(3) confirming valid third-party motor vehicle insurance.
A cover note issued by an authorised insurer that complies with prescribed requirements, serving as a temporary certificate of insurance before the formal certificate is issued.
Multiple certificates issued in connection with a single policy, or copies of a certificate, all of which together constitute the certificate of insurance.
Certificates issued by Government insurance funds authorised to carry on general insurance business under the General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972.
Attested photocopies of the certificate submitted within the prescribed fifteen-day period when the original is not in the possession of the owner or driver at the time of demand.
what_it_excludes: A mere policy of insurance document that has not been accompanied by the formal certificate issued under Section 147(3), as the policy alone does not satisfy the requirement.

Insurance certificates issued by entities that are not authorised insurers under the General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972, such as unauthorised or foreign insurers not notified for reciprocating countries.
A receipt or acknowledgment issued when a licence or document has been seized — this is specifically provided for driving licences, not certificates of insurance.
Comprehensive or own-damage insurance cover documents that do not include or confirm third-party liability cover as required under Chapter XI of the Act.
An expired insurance certificate where the policy period has lapsed, as it no longer constitutes valid proof of subsisting insurance cover for the vehicle.

definitions.definition: "Certificate of registration" means the certificate issued by a competent authority to the effect that a motor vehicle has been duly registered in accordance with the provisions of Chapter IV.
definitions.plain_english: A certificate of registration is an official document issued by the government's registering authority confirming that a motor vehicle has been legally registered as required by law. It serves as proof that the vehicle is recognised and permitted to be used on Indian roads. Without this certificate, a vehicle cannot be legally driven on public roads in India.
real_world_examples: A new car buyer in Mumbai receives a Registration Certificate (RC) from the Regional Transport Office (RTO) after paying registration fees and completing formalities, allowing the car to be driven on Maharashtra roads with the assigned number plate such as MH-01-AB-1234.

A truck owner in Delhi applies for a fresh certificate of registration after purchasing a second-hand heavy goods vehicle from a transporter in Haryana, and the RTO issues a new RC reflecting the change of ownership and the Delhi registration mark.

A two-wheeler owner in Chennai loses their original RC book and applies to the RTO for a duplicate certificate of registration, which is then issued bearing the same vehicle details and registration mark as the original.

A tourist vehicle operator in Rajasthan gets their vehicle's certificate of registration renewed after the prescribed validity period, ensuring the vehicle remains legally compliant for carrying passengers on tourist routes.

During a police check-post inspection on the Delhi-Agur highway, a commercial vehicle driver produces the certificate of registration to demonstrate that the vehicle is duly registered and authorised for use on public roads.

A car owner in Bengaluru who has made structural modifications to the vehicle applies for an updated certificate of registration reflecting the alterations, as required under Section 52 of the Motor Vehicles Act.
what_it_covers: Certificate issued by the registering authority (RTO) confirming that a private motor car has been duly registered under Chapter IV of the Motor Vehicles Act.
Certificate of registration issued for commercial transport vehicles such as buses, trucks, and taxis, confirming their registration and permissible gross vehicle weight.
Duplicate certificate of registration lawfully issued by the competent authority when the original is lost, stolen, or mutilated.
Certificate of registration issued for a newly manufactured or imported motor vehicle upon first registration in India.
Updated or amended certificate of registration issued after recording a change of ownership, alteration in vehicle structure, or change of address of the registered owner.
what_it_excludes: A temporary permit or transit document that may allow a vehicle to move between states but does not constitute formal registration under Chapter IV.
A certificate of fitness issued under Chapter IV, which certifies roadworthiness of a transport vehicle but is distinct from and does not replace the certificate of registration.
A dealer's delivery note or invoice issued at the time of purchase of a motor vehicle, which does not constitute registration by a competent authority.
An insurance certificate or cover note, which evidences insurance coverage but is not proof of registration of the vehicle.
A learner's licence or driving licence, which authorises a person to drive but has no bearing on whether the vehicle itself is registered.

The certificate of registration is also a prerequisite for obtaining a permit, insurance, and for establishing the identity and ownership of a vehicle in accident, theft, or transfer of ownership proceedings.

definitions.definition: A chassis includes a motor vehicle to which a body has not yet been attached, as expressly included within the definition of 'motor vehicle' under Section 2 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. It constitutes the structural framework of a motor vehicle, comprising the engine, transmission, and running gear, to which a body is subsequently fitted for use on roads.
definitions.plain_english: A chassis is the bare skeletal frame of a vehicle — including its engine and wheels — before any passenger cabin or cargo body has been bolted on. Think of it as the 'bare bones' of a truck or bus that comes out of a factory before the body builder adds the cabin or cargo area. Under the Motor Vehicles Act, even this incomplete structure is treated as a motor vehicle for legal purposes.
real_world_examples: A truck manufacturer in Pune dispatches a bare Tata or Ashok Leyland chassis (with engine and axles but no cargo body) to a body-builder workshop in Coimbatore; this chassis must be registered under the MV Act even though it has no completed body.

A bus operator in Delhi purchases a chassis from a manufacturer and sends it to a coach-building firm in Hyderabad to have a passenger body fitted; during transit on public roads, the chassis is legally a motor vehicle and requires valid registration and insurance.

A dealer in Mumbai displays and sells bare chassis of mini-trucks to customers who then commission custom bodies from local fabricators; the dealer's activities of selling chassis fall squarely within the definition of 'dealer' under the Act.

A road transport undertaking in Karnataka registers a chassis at the RTO before sending it for body fabrication, as required under Section 43 of the MV Act which mandates that even a bodyless chassis must carry registration marks and comply with registration requirements.

A custom body-builder in Chennai receives multiple chassis from a goods vehicle manufacturer and is classified as a 'dealer' under Section 2 because the Act expressly includes persons engaged in building bodies for attachment to chassis.
what_it_covers: A bare truck or bus chassis with engine, axles and wheels but without any superstructure or cargo/passenger body, dispatched from a manufacturer to a body-builder.
A chassis being driven or towed on public roads in India for the purpose of delivery to a body-builder workshop, even without a fitted cabin or cargo area.
A chassis held in stock by a dealer or manufacturer pending body construction, which is nonetheless subject to registration and other MV Act obligations.
A semi-finished vehicle framework on which assembly is partially complete but no enclosed body has been attached, making it legally equivalent to a motor vehicle.
A chassis used for testing or demonstration purposes on public roads by a manufacturer before body fitting.
what_it_excludes: A fully bodied and completed motor vehicle where the body has already been permanently attached and is ready for normal use on roads.
Spare parts, sub-assemblies or individual mechanical components (such as engines, axles, or gearboxes) that have not been assembled into a functional chassis framework.
A chassis confined entirely to a private factory or enclosed premises and never operated or moved on a public road, which may not attract road-use registration obligations.
A trailer frame that is not mechanically propelled and does not constitute a motor vehicle chassis within the meaning of the Act.
Non-motorised vehicle frames, such as those for bicycles or animal-drawn carts, which lack mechanical propulsion and fall entirely outside the MV Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Because a chassis is treated as a motor vehicle under the Act, it must be registered under Chapter IV (Section 43) even before a body is attached, meaning operating an unregistered chassis on public roads constitutes an offence. This classification also determines whether insurance, fitness certification, and permit obligations apply to a bodyless vehicle being moved between a manufacturer and a body-builder.

definitions.definition: A 'claim' under the Motor Vehicles Act means a demand or application made by an aggrieved person or their legal representatives for compensation or relief arising out of a motor accident, including claims for death, bodily injury, or property damage caused by the use of a motor vehicle, as adjudicated under Section 163B and related provisions governing no-fault liability.
definitions.plain_english: A 'claim' is a formal request made by an accident victim or their family to receive money as compensation after being hurt or killed in a road accident involving a motor vehicle. It is the legal step you take to ask for compensation from the vehicle owner, insurer, or a special tribunal. You do not always need to prove the other person was at fault to make such a claim.
real_world_examples: A pedestrian in Mumbai is struck by a speeding truck and suffers a broken leg; she files a claim before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal in Mumbai for medical expenses and loss of income under no-fault liability provisions.

The family of a Delhi autorickshaw driver who died when a private car jumped a red light files a claim before the MACT for compensation covering funeral costs, loss of dependency, and pain and suffering.
A school bus in Chennai meets with an accident injuring several students; the parents of the injured children individually file claims against the insurer of the bus under the Motor Vehicles Act.

A cyclist in Bengaluru is knocked down by a two-wheeler; having suffered permanent disability, he submits a claim petition to the Regional Claims Tribunal seeking structured compensation under Section 163B without having to prove negligence.

A widow in Kolkata whose husband was killed in a hit-and-run accident approaches the Solatium Fund scheme and files a claim for the prescribed lump-sum compensation as the vehicle owner could not be traced.
what_it_covers: A claim for compensation by the legal representatives of a person who died due to a motor accident under no-fault liability provisions of Section 163A/163B.
A claim by an accident victim for permanent disablement caused by the use of a motor vehicle, without requiring proof of negligence on the part of the driver or owner.
A claim made against an authorised insurer by a third party who suffered bodily injury or property damage caused by an insured motor vehicle.
A claim petition filed before the Claims Tribunal by the victim of a hit-and-run accident seeking compensation from the Solatium Fund.
A claim by a passenger injured while boarding, travelling in, or alighting from a stage carriage or contract carriage against the permit holder or their insurer.
what_it_excludes: A claim for pure property damage unconnected with any personal injury or death arising from use of a motor vehicle in a commercial dispute context.

An insurance claim for mechanical damage to one's own vehicle not involving any third-party bodily injury or death (i.e., own-damage claims under a comprehensive policy are outside the MACT jurisdiction).
A claim relating to ownership or title disputes over a motor vehicle, which falls under civil court jurisdiction and not under the Motor Vehicles Act claims framework.
A contractual claim under a hire-purchase or hypothecation agreement between a financier and a vehicle owner for default in loan repayment.
A claim for lost or unclaimed articles found in a transport vehicle, which is governed separately under Section 106 and does not constitute a 'claim' in the accident compensation sense.
definitions.why_it_matters: The characterisation of a demand as a 'claim' under the Motor Vehicles Act determines whether it falls within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Claims Tribunal, triggering the insurer's statutory obligation to indemnify, the no-fault liability caps under Section 163A/163B, and the time-limitation rules for filing; without this classification, the aggrieved party would have to seek remedy through ordinary civil courts with far more onerous procedural and evidentiary requirements.

definitions.definition: A 'cognizable offence' in the context of the Motor Vehicles Act refers to an offence in respect of which a police officer may, in accordance with the First Schedule of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, arrest without warrant. As used in Section 19, it denotes any such offence for the commission of which a motor vehicle has been used by the holder of a driving licence, thereby triggering the licensing authority's power to disqualify or revoke that licence.
definitions.plain_english: A cognizable offence is a serious crime where the police have the power to arrest someone without needing a warrant from a court. When someone uses a motor vehicle to commit such a crime — for example, using a car to transport stolen goods or to commit robbery — it falls under this category. Under the Motor Vehicles Act, if a driver uses their vehicle in such a crime, the licensing authority can cancel or suspend their driving licence.
real_world_examples: A driver in Mumbai uses his truck to transport stolen goods across state lines; since theft is a cognizable offence and a motor vehicle was used, the licensing authority can revoke his driving licence under Section 19.

A car owner in Delhi uses his vehicle to abduct a person (kidnapping being a cognizable offence under IPC); the licensing authority, upon receiving information from police, initiates proceedings to disqualify him from holding a driving licence.

In Bengaluru, a tempo driver is found to have used his vehicle to smuggle narcotic drugs across districts; as drug trafficking is a cognizable offence, the RTO can revoke his commercial driving licence.

A taxi driver in Chennai is involved in a hit-and-run accident resulting in grievous hurt and flees the scene; since causing grievous hurt by rash driving is cognizable, the licensing authority proceeds to disqualify him from driving.

A truck operator in Hyderabad uses his heavy goods vehicle to illegally transport arms and ammunition; as offences under the Arms Act are cognizable, the licensing authority cancels his driving licence upon conviction.
what_it_covers: Offences such as robbery, kidnapping, murder, or dacoity where a motor vehicle is used as an instrument or means of committing the crime.
Drug trafficking or smuggling of contraband carried out using a motor vehicle, as offences under the NDPS Act are cognizable.
Causing death or grievous hurt by rash and negligent driving where the offence is classified as cognizable under the CrPC schedule.
Use of a vehicle for commission of offences under the Arms Act, such as illegal transport of weapons, which are cognizable in nature.
Using a motor vehicle in the commission of offences related to human trafficking, which are cognizable and warrant police intervention without prior court approval.
what_it_excludes: Non-cognizable offences such as minor traffic infractions (e.g., parking violations, minor document irregularities) where police cannot arrest without a warrant.
Civil wrongs or tortious acts involving a motor vehicle, such as causing property damage through negligence that does not amount to a criminal cognizable offence.
Bailable and non-cognizable offences under traffic regulations where the licensing authority's power to disqualify under Section 19(1)(c) is not specifically triggered.
Mere suspicion or allegation of a cognizable offence without the licensing authority being satisfied of actual use of the vehicle in the commission of such offence.
Administrative or regulatory violations under the Motor Vehicles Act itself that are specifically listed as non-cognizable offences in the Act's schedules.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an offence qualifies as a 'cognizable offence' directly determines whether Section 19(1)(c) can be invoked by the licensing authority to disqualify a person from holding a driving licence or to revoke an existing licence. If the offence is non-cognizable, this specific ground for revocation or disqualification is unavailable, and the licensing authority must rely on other listed grounds under Section 19.

definitions.definition: The Collector refers to the District Collector or the Revenue Collector of a district, being the principal revenue officer of the district empowered under the Motor Vehicles Act to receive certificates issued by the Claims Tribunal and to recover amounts awarded thereunder in the same manner as an arrear of land revenue.
definitions.plain_english: The Collector is the senior government revenue official of a district — typically known as the District Collector or Deputy Commissioner — who is responsible for collecting money that has been awarded by a motor accident claims tribunal but not paid by the person or insurer who owes it. When someone wins a compensation award from the tribunal but cannot get the money, the Collector steps in and recovers it using the same powerful methods used to collect unpaid land taxes. This makes enforcement of motor accident compensation much faster and more effective.
real_world_examples: A road accident victim in Pune wins a compensation award of ₹8 lakhs from the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal against an insurer, but the insurer refuses to pay. The victim applies to the tribunal, which issues a certificate to the District Collector of Pune, who then recovers the amount by attaching the insurer's property as if it were unpaid land revenue.

A family in rural Rajasthan loses their breadwinner in a truck accident and receives a MACT award of ₹15 lakhs. When the truck owner fails to pay, the Claims Tribunal issues a certificate to the Collector of the concerned district, who uses revenue recovery powers to attach the truck owner's agricultural land and recover the dues.

In Chennai, after a fatal hit-and-run case, the Claims Tribunal awards compensation from the Solatium Fund. The Collector of Chennai district is directed to recover contributions from the registered insurer who has defaulted, treating the outstanding amount as arrear of land revenue under Section 174.

A pedestrian injured in a bus accident in Lucknow obtains an award from the MACT but the state transport undertaking delays payment. The victim files an application before the tribunal, which issues a recovery certificate to the Collector of Lucknow, who proceeds to enforce payment using land revenue recovery mechanisms including attachment and sale of government assets.

In a commercial vehicle accident in Hyderabad, multiple victims receive a joint award. When the owner-cum-driver is untraceable and the insurer disputes liability, the tribunal issues certificates to the District Collector of Hyderabad to recover dues from whatever assets of the insurer are available in the district.
what_it_covers: The District Collector or Deputy Commissioner of a district who is the principal revenue officer empowered to recover MACT awards as land revenue arrears.
Any Additional Collector or officer holding charge of the Collector's office and exercising revenue recovery powers under applicable state revenue laws.
The Collector of the district where the defaulting party's property or assets are situated, to whom the Claims Tribunal may issue a recovery certificate under Section 174.
A Collector acting in a district where an insurer or vehicle owner has moveable or immoveable property that can be attached and sold for recovery of the awarded amount.
what_it_excludes: Private debt collection agents or agencies — the Collector is exclusively a government revenue official and no private entity can exercise these statutory recovery powers.
Judicial officers such as civil court judges or magistrates, who are separate from the revenue hierarchy and do not exercise land revenue recovery powers under this provision.
Officers of insurance companies or the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority (IRDAI), who are not vested with any land revenue recovery authority.
Tax Collectors under the Income Tax Act or GST officers, who function under entirely different statutory frameworks and cannot act as Collectors for purposes of Section 174.
State Transport Authorities or licensing authorities under the MV Act, whose functions relate to permits and licences, not revenue recovery of award amounts.
definitions.why_it_matters: The applicability of the Collector definition determines whether a MACT award can be enforced using the swift and coercive land revenue recovery mechanism under Section 174, bypassing the slower civil court execution process; if this definition applies, the Collector can attach and sell the defaulter's property without a separate civil suit, ensuring timely compensation to accident victims. Failure to route recovery through the Collector in the prescribed manner may render the enforcement of an award legally ineffective or delayed.

definitions.definition: A 'commercial enterprise' refers to any activity or undertaking carried on for the purpose of trade, profit, or business gain. As used in the Motor Vehicles Act, a vehicle is connected with a commercial enterprise when it is employed in or for the furtherance of any such profit-oriented activity, as distinguished from purely governmental or public-purpose use unconnected with trade or commerce.
definitions.plain_english: A commercial enterprise simply means any business or profit-making activity. In the context of the Motor Vehicles Act, it is used to draw a line between government vehicles used purely for official or defence purposes and those used for earning money or running a business. If a government vehicle is used for any trade or money-making purpose, it loses certain exemptions available only to non-commercial government vehicles.
real_world_examples: An Indian Army truck used to transport military supplies and equipment along the Line of Control is NOT connected with any commercial enterprise, and is therefore exempt from requiring a transport permit under Section 66.

A vehicle owned by the Ministry of Defence but rented out to a private logistics company for transporting goods for a fee IS connected with a commercial enterprise and would not qualify for exemptions under Sections 18, 60, or 66.

A Central Government-owned bus used to ferry defence personnel between a cantonment and a military base, with no charge levied, is unconnected with commercial enterprise and may be registered under Section 60 without standard registration requirements.

A vehicle belonging to the Border Roads Organisation (BRO) used to construct highways for commercial toll-road projects operated under a public-private partnership could be considered connected with a commercial enterprise, thereby disqualifying it from exemptions available to purely defence-purpose vehicles.

A Navy-owned utility van used exclusively to transport naval officers on official duty is unconnected with any commercial enterprise, and the driver may hold a driving licence issued under Section 18 rather than a standard commercial driving licence.
what_it_covers: A Central Government vehicle used to transport goods or passengers for a fee or hire, thereby generating revenue or profit.
A government-owned vehicle deployed in support of a state-run trading or manufacturing corporation engaged in commercial production and sale.
A Defence Ministry vehicle leased or contracted out to a private entity for haulage, logistics, or any revenue-generating transportation activity.

definitions.definition: "company" means any body corporate and includes a firm or other association of individuals; and "director", in relation to a firm, means a partner in the firm.
definitions.plain_english: A 'company' under the Motor Vehicles Act refers to any legally recognised corporate body, as well as partnerships and other groups of individuals acting together as a unit. This broad definition ensures that not only private or public limited companies but also partnership firms and unregistered associations are covered under relevant provisions of the Act. The term is used primarily in contexts dealing with corporate liability, insurance, and ownership of motor vehicles.
real_world_examples: A private limited company such as Ola Fleet Technologies Pvt. Ltd. registered under the Companies Act that owns a fleet of cab vehicles and holds permits under the Motor Vehicles Act is considered a 'company' for the purposes of Sections 71 and 151.

A partnership firm running a transport business in Punjab under the name 'Singh Brothers Transport' is treated as a 'company' under the MV Act, making all its partners jointly liable for any violations or compensation claims arising under the Act.

An unregistered association of truck owners in Maharashtra pooling vehicles under a cooperative arrangement qualifies as an 'association of individuals' and thus a 'company' for the purposes of liability under Section 199.

A public sector undertaking like the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation (KSRTC), being a body corporate established by statute, falls within the definition of 'company' and is subject to the corporate liability provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act.

A logistics company incorporated as a Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) operating goods carriages across multiple states is treated as a 'company' for the purposes of permit conditions and insurance obligations under Section 153.
what_it_covers: Private limited companies and public limited companies registered under the Companies Act that own or operate motor vehicles.
Partnership firms engaged in transport or goods carriage business, where each partner is treated as a 'director' for the purposes of the Act.
Unregistered associations of individuals jointly owning or operating motor vehicles for commercial purposes.
Statutory bodies and public sector corporations constituted as bodies corporate, such as State Road Transport Undertakings.
Limited Liability Partnerships (LLPs) operating fleets of vehicles under permits granted by transport authorities.
what_it_excludes: Individual natural persons owning or driving motor vehicles in their personal capacity, who are governed as 'owners' or 'drivers' rather than as a 'company'.
Government departments that are not constituted as separate bodies corporate (e.g., a state PWD department using vehicles is not a 'company' in this sense).
Hindu Undivided Families (HUFs) acting as vehicle owners, as they are not a body corporate, firm, or association of individuals in the statutory sense contemplated by this definition.
Sole proprietorships, where a single individual trades under a business name without forming any partnership or corporate structure.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'company' determines which entities can be held corporately liable under Sections 71, 151, 153, and 199 of the Motor Vehicles Act, including liability for offences committed by their employees or agents and obligations relating to permits, insurance, and compensation. Misclassification of an entity as a non-company could shield it from prosecution under Section 199, which imposes specific penalties on companies and their directors or partners for contraventions of the Act.

definitions.definition: Compensation means the monetary amount payable to a person or their legal representatives on account of death, permanent disablement, bodily injury, or loss arising from an accident involving a motor vehicle, or on account of cancellation or modification of a permit by a State transport undertaking, determined either as a fixed sum under the no-fault principle, or as assessed by a Claims Tribunal on the basis of fault, wrongful act, neglect, or default, in accordance with the provisions of this Act.
definitions.plain_english: Compensation is the money that must be paid to a victim (or their family) when someone is killed or injured in a motor vehicle accident, or to a permit holder when their permit is cancelled or changed by the government transport authority. It can be a fixed amount paid without needing to prove anyone's fault, or a larger amount awarded by a tribunal after examining who was responsible. The goal is to provide financial relief to those who have suffered a loss due to a motor vehicle-related event.
real_world_examples: A pedestrian in Mumbai is struck and killed by a private bus; the bus owner is required to pay a fixed compensation of fifty thousand rupees to the deceased's family under the no-fault principle of Section 140, regardless of whether the driver was negligent.

A truck driver in Punjab is permanently disabled after a road accident caused by a rash driver; the Claims Tribunal in Chandigarh awards compensation assessed on the basis of the driver's income, age, and degree of disability after examining fault under Section 168.

A stage carriage permit holder in Karnataka has his permit cancelled by the State transport undertaking to nationalise a route; he is paid compensation calculated at two hundred rupees per complete month of the unexpired permit period for each affected vehicle under Section 105.

A family in Delhi whose breadwinner died in a hit-and-run accident applies to the Claims Tribunal under Section 166 for compensation; the tribunal assesses and awards an amount based on the deceased's salary, age, and number of dependants.

A goods vehicle owner in Tamil Nadu whose permit area is curtailed by the Regional Transport Authority receives proportional compensation computed using the YA/R formula under Section 105(5) for the reduction in route length.

An auto-rickshaw passenger in Hyderabad suffers grievous hurt when the vehicle overturns; the insurer of the vehicle is directed by the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal to pay compensation covering medical expenses and loss of income under Sections 165 and 166.
what_it_covers: Fixed sum of fifty thousand rupees payable to legal representatives upon death of a person in a motor vehicle accident under the no-fault principle (Section 140).
Fixed sum of twenty-five thousand rupees payable to a person who suffers permanent disablement due to a motor vehicle accident without requiring proof of fault (Section 140).
Amount awarded by a Claims Tribunal for death, bodily injury, or property damage arising from a motor vehicle accident on the basis of wrongful act, neglect, or default (Sections 165, 166, 168).

Monetary payment made by a State transport undertaking to a permit holder whose permit is cancelled or modified for purposes of route nationalisation, calculated at two hundred rupees per complete month of unexpired permit period (Section 105).
Proportional compensation for curtailment of a permit's area or route, calculated using the YA/R statutory formula (Section 105(5)).
Interest at seven per cent per annum payable on compensation when a State transport undertaking delays payment beyond one month (Section 105(6)).
what_it_excludes: Compensation on account of refusal to renew a permit under Section 103(2)(a) — explicitly excluded by Section 105(3).
Compensation where the permit holder has accepted an alternative route or area offered in lieu of the cancelled or modified permit (Section 105(2)).
Punitive fines, penalties, or prosecution costs levied under the Act for traffic offences, which are not compensation but criminal or regulatory sanctions.
Gratuity, pension, or employment benefits payable under labour laws such as the Workmen's Compensation Act 1923, which operate independently unless reduced from the award under Section 140(5).

Compensation for damage to the motor vehicle itself when claimed by the vehicle's own owner against their own insurer under a comprehensive policy, as the Act primarily governs third-party and accident victim claims.
Solatium payments under hit-and-run provisions, which are governed separately under Section 161 and the Solatium Fund scheme and are distinct from full compensation awards.
definitions.why_it_matters: The determination of whether an amount qualifies as 'compensation' under this Act governs which tribunal has jurisdiction to adjudicate the claim (Claims Tribunal under Sections 165–168), whether the no-fault fixed sum is payable immediately without proof of negligence (Section 140), and whether an insurer is obligated to indemnify the owner — directly affecting the enforceability of claims against owners and insurers and the quantum of relief available to accident victims and permit holders.

definitions.definition: The competency test to drive refers to the test of competence to drive as referred to in sub-section (3) of section 9 of the Motor Vehicles Act, which a person convicted of an offence punishable under section 184 (dangerous driving) may be required to pass subsequent to an order of disqualification, to the satisfaction of the licensing authority, before the disqualification is lifted.
definitions.plain_english: A competency test to drive is a formal driving skill and knowledge test administered by the licensing authority, which a person must pass before they can get their driving licence back after being disqualified by a court for dangerous driving. Even if the person had passed such a test before, the court can order them to take and pass it again after the disqualification period. The licensing authority must be satisfied with the test result before restoring the licence.
real_world_examples: A driver in Mumbai is convicted of dangerous driving under section 184 after jumping multiple red lights and causing an accident; the court disqualifies him and further orders that he must re-appear for the driving competency test at the RTO before his licence can be restored, regardless of the fact that he had originally passed the test 10 years ago.

A truck driver in Delhi is convicted under section 184 for overtaking recklessly on NH-44, causing a multi-vehicle pile-up; the court orders a disqualification period and conditions restoration of his heavy goods vehicle licence on successfully passing the competency test again at the licensing authority.

A young car owner in Bengaluru, convicted of dangerous driving after racing on ORR, is disqualified by the Magistrate's Court and directed to pass the competency test to drive at the jurisdictional RTO before any driving licence is reissued to him.

A commercial taxi driver in Chennai whose licence was suspended by court order under section 184 approaches the licensing authority after the disqualification period ends, but is informed he must first pass the competency test to drive — including practical driving and road rules components — before his licence can be reinstated.

A repeat offender in Hyderabad, previously convicted under section 184, is again convicted and disqualified; the Sessions Court explicitly records in its order that the person must pass the competency test to the satisfaction of the licensing authority before the disqualification can be lifted, even though he holds a valid driving history spanning 15 years.
what_it_covers: The formal test of competence to drive administered under sub-section (3) of section 9 of the Motor Vehicles Act, assessing both theoretical knowledge and practical driving ability.

Persons convicted under section 184 (dangerous driving) who are directed by the court to pass the test subsequent to a disqualification order, irrespective of whether they had previously passed such a test.

Assessment conducted by or to the satisfaction of the licensing authority, including evaluation of a driver's fitness to safely operate the specific class or description of vehicle mentioned in their licence.
what_it_excludes: The initial competency test taken by a first-time applicant for a driving licence under section 9, which is not the same as the court-ordered post-disqualification test under section 20.
Learner's licence tests or provisional driving assessments, which do not constitute the competency test to drive as used in the context of section 20.
Medical fitness examinations or eye-sight tests required separately under the Act, which are distinct from the competency test to drive and do not substitute for it.

Disqualification orders made under sections other than section 184 (e.g., under sections 132, 134, or 185), where the court is not specifically empowered to impose the competency test condition as a prerequisite for licence restoration.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a convicted person is required to pass the competency test to drive directly determines when and whether their driving licence can be restored after a court-ordered disqualification — failure to pass the test means the disqualification continues regardless of the expiry of the specified disqualification period. This condition is triggered specifically by conviction under section 184 (dangerous driving) and is imposed at the court's discretion, making it a critical element of the judicial penalty framework under the Motor Vehicles Act.

definitions.definition: "Conductor", in relation to a stage carriage, means a person engaged in collecting fares from passengers, regulating their entrance into, or exit from, the stage carriage and performing such other functions as may be prescribed.
definitions.plain_english: A conductor is the person on a bus (stage carriage) whose job is to collect ticket fares from passengers and manage passengers getting on and off the bus. They may also carry out additional duties as required by the rules. They are distinct from the driver and must hold a separate conductor's licence to perform this role legally.
real_world_examples: A ticket collector on a Delhi Transport Corporation (DTC) red bus who issues paper tickets, collects cash fares, and signals the driver when it is safe for passengers to board or alight at a bus stop.
A person employed by a Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation (KSRTC) interstate bus who manages passenger boarding at each stop, collects fares, and maintains records of passengers on the route.
An individual working on a private stage carriage operating between two towns in Maharashtra who collects fares, issues receipts, and ensures orderly entry and exit of passengers at designated stops.
A conductor on a Uttar Pradesh roadways bus who checks that passengers have valid tickets or passes, collects fares from those without tickets, and manages the rush of passengers during peak hours.

A person employed by a Tamil Nadu State Transport Corporation bus who uses a digital ticketing machine to issue e-tickets, regulates passenger flow at bus stands, and ensures safety during boarding and deboarding.
what_it_covers: A person employed on a stage carriage (public bus) who collects fares from passengers during the journey.
A person who regulates and manages the entry and exit of passengers at bus stops along the route of a stage carriage.
A bus staff member performing any additional functions prescribed under the Motor Vehicles Act or state transport rules, such as maintaining passenger records or issuing tickets.
A conductor employed by either a state road transport undertaking or a private operator running a stage carriage on a licensed route.
what_it_excludes: The driver of the stage carriage, who is separately defined under the Act and requires a driving licence rather than a conductor's licence.
Personnel on a contract carriage or private service vehicle, as the definition is expressly limited to persons working on a stage carriage only.
A person employed purely as a security guard or cleaner on a bus who does not collect fares or regulate passenger boarding and alighting.
An inspector or supervisor of a transport company who oversees operations but does not personally collect fares or manage passenger entry and exit on the vehicle.
Persons operating maxicabs or motorcabs, since these are not classified as stage carriages under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a conductor directly determines whether they must hold a valid conductor's licence under Chapter III of the Act, and failure to do so attracts penalties under sections such as Section 178; it also triggers obligations relating to licensing, conduct rules, disqualification, and liability under Sections 29, 30, 33, 37, 38, and related provisions.

definitions.definition: "Conductor's licence" means the licence issued by a competent authority under Chapter III authorising the person specified therein to act as a conductor.
definitions.plain_english: A conductor's licence is an official permit issued by the government that allows a specific person to work as a conductor on a stage carriage (public bus). Without this licence, a person cannot legally collect fares, manage passenger boarding and alighting, or perform other conductor duties on a public bus. definitions.definition: For the purposes of section 42, 'consular officer' means any person who is recognised as such by the Central Government, and if any question arises as to whether a person is or is not such an officer, the decision of the Central Government thereon shall be final.
definitions.plain_english: A consular officer is a foreign government representative—such as a Consul General, Consul, or Vice-Consul—officially recognised by the Indian Central Government as holding that diplomatic status. The Central Government has the final say in deciding whether any particular person qualifies as a consular officer. Such officers receive special treatment when registering motor vehicles in India, including distinct registration marks and a simplified procedure.
real_world_examples: The Consul General of France posted in Mumbai applies for registration of an official vehicle; the RTO registers it under Section 42 with a special CD/CC-series registration mark instead of the standard MH-series number.

A German Vice-Consul stationed in Chennai purchases a new car; because the Central Government has recognised her as a consular officer, her vehicle is exempt from the usual registration requirements under sections 39 and 40 as long as the car remains her property.

A Consulate of Japan in Kolkata acquires an additional official vehicle; under Section 42, the registering authority follows Central Government rules rather than the standard sub-sections (3) and (6) of Section 41, issuing a special certificate of registration.

A person claiming consular status for a vehicle registration in Delhi is disputed by the RTO; the matter is referred to the Central Government, whose decision on whether the person qualifies as a consular officer is treated as final and binding.

A consular officer from the Brazilian Consulate in Bengaluru sells his registered vehicle to a local Indian citizen; upon the transfer of ownership, the special certificate of registration under Section 42 ceases to be effective and normal registration requirements under sections 39 and 40 immediately apply to the new owner.
what_it_covers: A Consul General, Consul, Vice-Consul, or Honorary Consul of a foreign country who is formally recognised by the Indian Central Government in that capacity.
Any consular staff member individually recognised by the Central Government as a consular officer, regardless of rank or nationality of the posting country.
Any person whose consular status is disputed but whose recognition by the Central Government has been affirmatively confirmed through the Central Government's final determination.
Consular officers from countries without full diplomatic relations with India, provided the Central Government has extended specific recognition to them as consular officers.
what_it_excludes: Ordinary administrative or clerical staff of a foreign consulate who have not been individually recognised as 'consular officers' by the Central Government.
Honorary consular agents who have not received formal recognition from the Central Government, even if recognised under their home country's law.
Indian nationals working within a foreign consulate in a local staff capacity, as they would not be recognised as foreign consular officers.
Persons who were previously recognised as consular officers but whose recognition has been withdrawn or who have completed their posting and left India.
Diplomatic officers (Ambassadors, High Commissioners, etc.), who fall under a separate but parallel category in Section 42 and are governed by the definition of 'diplomatic officer'.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a 'consular officer' under Section 42 determines whether their motor vehicle can be registered under the special Central Government procedure with a distinctive registration mark, exempting it from the standard registration requirements of sections 39 and 40 of the Motor Vehicles Act for as long as the vehicle remains their property. If the definition does not apply—either because recognition is absent or has lapsed—the vehicle becomes subject to ordinary registration obligations, and operating it without such registration constitutes an offence under the Act.

definitions.definition: "contract carriage" means a motor vehicle which carries a passenger or passengers for hire or reward and is engaged under a contract, whether expressed or implied, for the use of such vehicle as a whole for the carriage of passengers mentioned therein and entered into by a person with a holder of a permit in relation to such vehicle or any person authorised by him in this behalf on a fixed or an agreed rate or sum—on a time basis, whether or not with reference to any route or distance; or from one point to another, and in either case, without stopping to pick up or set down passengers not included in the contract anywhere during the journey, and includes—(i) a maxicab; and (ii) a motor cab notwithstanding that separate fares are charged for its passengers.
definitions.plain_english: A contract carriage is a vehicle hired by a person or group under a private agreement to carry only those specific passengers named in the contract, for a fixed price or agreed rate. The key feature is that the vehicle is booked as a whole — not for individual seats — and it cannot stop to pick up or drop off any passengers who are not part of the original booking. Common examples include hired taxis, school trip buses, and wedding coaches.
real_world_examples: A company in Bengaluru hires a 40-seater bus under a monthly contract to ferry its employees from specific residential areas to the office and back every day — the bus cannot pick up random passengers along the route.

A family in Jaipur books an Ola or Uber cab (motorcab) through an app for a fixed fare to travel from their home to Jaipur airport — this constitutes a contract carriage even though the app charges a per-ride fare.

A school in Mumbai hires a maxicab on an annual contract to transport students from a particular locality to the school and back, with a fixed monthly payment to the permit holder — the vehicle cannot carry other passengers during the trip.

A group of tourists in Kerala privately charters a tempo traveller (maxicab) from a travel agency for a 5-day tour across the state at an agreed lump-sum amount — this is a contract carriage operating on a time basis.

A wedding party in Delhi books a fleet of Innova cars to transport guests from the hotel to the banquet hall and back under a negotiated package rate with a transport operator — each car qualifies as a contract carriage for the duration of the engagement.
what_it_covers: A maxicab (vehicle carrying 7 to 12 passengers excluding driver) hired under a contract for a specific group journey.
A motorcab (vehicle carrying up to 6 passengers excluding driver) like an app-based or metered taxi, even when separate fares are charged per passenger.
A tourist bus or coach chartered by a travel agency for a group tour on a fixed lump-sum or daily rate basis.
An employee shuttle bus hired by a corporate under a monthly contract for exclusive use of its staff between fixed points.
A vehicle booked on a time basis (e.g., hourly or daily hire) without a predetermined route, used solely for the contracting party's passengers.
what_it_excludes: A stage carriage, which operates on a fixed route and schedule and is authorised to pick up and set down passengers at designated stops along the journey.

A private service vehicle used for carrying passengers without hire or reward (e.g., a vehicle owned and used by a company exclusively for its own staff without any payment arrangement constituting hire).
A goods carriage, which is constructed or adapted solely for the transport of goods rather than passengers.
An educational institution bus owned by a school or college and used solely for transporting its own students or staff, which is separately categorised under the Act.
A vehicle engaged in road transport under a state transport undertaking operating regular public services on notified routes.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a vehicle qualifies as a contract carriage directly determines the type of permit required under Chapter V — a contract carriage permit under Sections 66, 74, and 80 — and operating without such a permit or picking up non-contracted passengers constitutes a punishable offence under Section 192A. It also governs the applicable insurance requirements, fare regulation, and the conditions under which the vehicle may legally operate.

definitions.definition: A permit in respect of a contract carriage, as referred to in Chapter V of the Motor Vehicles Act, granted by a Regional Transport Authority on an application made under Section 73, authorising the use of a vehicle as a contract carriage in accordance with specified conditions including the type and seating capacity of the vehicle and the area of operation.
definitions.plain_english: A contract carriage permit is an official licence issued by a Regional Transport Authority that allows a vehicle owner to operate a vehicle for hire on a private, pre-arranged basis — meaning the entire vehicle is hired by one party rather than individual seats being sold to the general public. The permit specifies where the vehicle can operate, how many passengers it can carry, and the conditions under which it can be hired. Examples include permits for taxis, app-based cabs, tourist coaches, and school buses hired as a whole.
real_world_examples: A Delhi-based taxi operator running an Ola or Uber cab under a contract carriage permit that authorises him to ply the vehicle within the National Capital Region for point-to-point hire by individual customers.

A travel agency in Mumbai obtaining a contract carriage permit for a 40-seater air-conditioned coach to ferry corporate employees from residential colonies to office campuses under a fixed monthly contract.

A Kerala State Road Transport Corporation subsidiary applying for a contract carriage permit for tourist vehicles used to transport foreign visitors on pre-booked pilgrimage circuits to temples across the state.
An ex-serviceman in Pune receiving preferential grant of a contract carriage permit for a maxicab used to carry wedding parties and private groups within Pune district under a hire agreement.

A State transport undertaking in Karnataka applying under Section 103 for a contract carriage permit in respect of a notified route for operating luxury coaches, with the Regional Transport Authority issuing the permit notwithstanding competing private applications.
what_it_covers: A permit granted to a motor cab operator authorising point-to-point hire within a specified area or on specified routes.
A permit issued to a State transport undertaking under Section 103 in respect of a notified area or notified route for operating contract carriages notwithstanding Chapter V provisions.
A permit for a maxi-cab or tourist coach hired as a whole by a single hirer under a pre-arranged contract, with conditions on maximum passengers, luggage, and rates of hiring.
Permits with attached conditions such as fitment of a taximeter, display of fare tables, and maintenance of cleanliness standards as prescribed by the Regional Transport Authority.
what_it_excludes: Stage carriage permits, which authorise the carriage of passengers at separate fares on fixed routes open to the general public rather than under a private hire contract.
Goods carriage permits, which authorise the transportation of goods rather than passengers under a contract carriage arrangement.
Private service vehicles used exclusively for carrying employees of an organisation without hire or reward, which do not require a contract carriage permit.
Vehicles operating under a national permit for goods carriage, which fall under a separate permit category governed by different provisions of the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a vehicle is operating under a valid contract carriage permit determines whether its operation is lawful under Chapter V of the Motor Vehicles Act; operating without such a permit constitutes an offence attracting penalties, and the permit's conditions — including area, route, passenger limits, and fare structures — define the precise scope of lawful hire operations. Under Section 103, possession of a contract carriage permit by a State transport undertaking in respect of a notified route enables it to override competing private operators and empowers the transport authority to cancel or restrict existing private permits.
