definitions.definition: For the purposes of sections 150, 151 and 152 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 'liabilities to third parties' in relation to a person insured under any policy of insurance means the liabilities of that insured person towards third parties arising under or covered by that policy, but does not include any liability of that person in the capacity of insurer under some other policy of insurance.
definitions.plain_english: This term refers to the financial responsibilities that an insured person has towards other people (third parties) who may be harmed or suffer loss due to the insured's actions or vehicle — for example, paying compensation to accident victims. However, if the same insured person also happens to be an insurance company and owes money under a separate insurance policy they issued, that obligation is not counted here. Essentially, it covers what the insured owes to outsiders as a result of their own actions, not what they owe in their role as an insurer.
real_world_examples: A truck driver in Maharashtra injures a pedestrian in a road accident; the trucking company's insurer must cover the compensation payable to the pedestrian — this compensation obligation is a 'liability to third parties' under the insured trucking company's motor vehicle policy.

A Delhi-based private car owner's vehicle rams into a roadside shop, damaging property and injuring the shopkeeper; the car owner's insurer is liable to cover the shopkeeper's medical expenses and property damage, which constitute liabilities to third parties.

A state transport bus in Tamil Nadu meets with an accident injuring several passengers from another vehicle; the bus operator's insurer must indemnify those injured road users — these obligations are liabilities to third parties.

An insurance company (General Insurance Corporation) itself owns a fleet of vehicles and holds a motor insurance policy for them; if one of its vehicles causes harm to a bystander, the compensation owed to the bystander is a liability to third parties, but if the same insurance company separately issued a life policy and owes a death claim under that policy, that separate insurance obligation is excluded from the definition.

A goods vehicle operator in Punjab carrying goods for a client is involved in a collision injuring occupants of another car; the insurer of the goods vehicle is obligated to cover the injured car occupants' claims — these are liabilities to third parties covered under sections 150–152.
what_it_covers: Compensation payable by an insured vehicle owner or driver to pedestrians, cyclists, or occupants of other vehicles injured in a road accident.
Property damage claims by third parties (e.g., damaged roadside structures, other vehicles) arising from the insured's vehicle involvement in an accident.
Medical and rehabilitation expenses owed by an insured person to injured third parties as determined by a Claims Tribunal under the Motor Vehicles Act.
Death compensation payable to the legal heirs of a third party killed in a motor accident caused by the insured person's vehicle.
what_it_excludes: Any liability owed by an insured person in their capacity as an insurer under a separate policy of insurance issued by them — explicitly excluded by Section 153.

Liabilities arising in the context of a voluntary winding up of a company undertaken solely for reconstruction or amalgamation with another company, as sections 150, 151 and 152 do not apply in such cases.
Internal or contractual liabilities between the insured and their own employees or co-insured parties that do not constitute third-party claims.
Liabilities arising under a separate non-motor insurance policy (such as life, health, or property insurance) even if the same entity holds a motor vehicle policy.
definitions.why_it_matters: The scope of 'liabilities to third parties' determines which obligations an insurer must honour when an insured person becomes insolvent or a company is wound up under sections 150, 151 and 152, thereby protecting accident victims' rights to compensation even in insolvency scenarios. If a liability falls outside this definition — such as one arising from the insured acting as an insurer — the statutory transfer of rights under sections 150–152 does not apply, potentially leaving that obligation outside the protective insolvency framework.

definitions.definition: 'liability', wherever used in relation to the death of or bodily injury to any person, includes liability in respect thereof under section 140.
definitions.plain_english: In the context of motor vehicle insurance under the Motor Vehicles Act, 'liability' refers to the legal obligation of a vehicle owner or insurer to pay compensation when someone is killed or physically injured in a motor accident. This obligation explicitly includes the no-fault liability imposed under Section 140, meaning compensation can be claimed even without proving negligence or wrongdoing by the owner. Essentially, it is the financial and legal responsibility that arises from death or bodily harm caused by the use of a motor vehicle.
real_world_examples: A bus belonging to a private operator in Pune knocks down a pedestrian at a busy crossing, causing grievous injuries. The owner's insurer is liable to pay compensation under both the no-fault principle (Section 140) and under tort law, and this combined obligation falls within the definition of 'liability' as used in the insurance chapter.

A motorcyclist in Delhi dies in a collision with a truck. The truck owner's insurer is required to honour the 'liability' under the policy, which includes the fixed no-fault compensation of fifty thousand rupees to the deceased's family under Section 140, regardless of whether the truck driver was at fault.

A passenger travelling in a contract carriage (tourist bus) in Rajasthan suffers permanent disablement in an accident. The insurer's 'liability' covers the mandatory no-fault compensation of twenty-five thousand rupees under Section 140, in addition to any further damages awarded by the Claims Tribunal.

A stage carriage operator in Chennai tries to insert a clause in the passenger ticket disclaiming all responsibility for injury during travel. Under Section 92, such a clause is void, and the operator's 'liability' for bodily injury to passengers remains intact and enforceable under the Act.

In a hit-and-run accident in Mumbai where a goods vehicle injures a roadside vendor, even if the owner temporarily evades identification, the concept of 'liability' ensures that compensation obligations exist and can be pursued through the Solatium Fund or against the insurer once the vehicle is traced.
what_it_covers: Liability of a vehicle owner to pay fixed no-fault compensation under Section 140 in cases of death or permanent disablement arising from a motor accident, irrespective of any negligence.
Liability of an authorised insurer under a valid policy of insurance to indemnify the insured owner against claims for death or bodily injury to third parties or passengers.

Liability arising from bodily injury to a passenger of a stage carriage or contract carriage while boarding, travelling in, or alighting from the vehicle, which cannot be contractually excluded under Section 92.
Liability that attaches jointly and severally to multiple owners of vehicles involved in the same accident causing death or permanent disablement.
Liability of a vehicle owner for death or bodily injury that may also attract compensation under other laws (e.g., Workmen's Compensation Act), subject to adjustment of amounts.
what_it_excludes: Liability solely for damage to property (such as roads, bridges, or goods carried), which is governed separately and not covered by this specific definition focused on death or bodily injury.

Contractual liability that has been voided or negated by an agreement between the operator and passenger — such contracts are void under Section 92 and do not constitute enforceable 'liability' under the Act.

Liability of the Central Government or State Government vehicles used for non-commercial Government purposes, which are exempt from the mandatory insurance requirement under Section 146(2) and therefore outside the insurance-linked liability framework.

Pure civil or criminal liability for rash or negligent driving under other penal statutes (e.g., IPC), which is distinct from the specific statutory 'liability' as defined in Section 145 of this Chapter.
Liability arising from damage or loss to the motor vehicle itself (own damage), as this definition is exclusively restricted to death or bodily injury to persons.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'liability' determines the minimum scope of what an authorised insurer must cover under a compulsory third-party insurance policy — if a claim falls within this definition, the insurer cannot refuse indemnification on the ground that fault was not proven, because Section 140 no-fault liability is expressly included. It also governs the obligations imposed on vehicle owners and insurers in Sections 151 and 152, where insurers are required to satisfy judgments related to this liability even in cases of policy breach by the insured.

definitions.term: liability covered by the terms of the policy
definitions.definition: The expression 'liability covered by the terms of the policy' means a liability which is covered by the policy or which would be so covered but for the fact that the insurer is entitled to avoid or cancel or has avoided or cancelled the policy.
definitions.plain_english: This term refers to any legal liability that an insurance policy either actually covers, or would have covered if the insurer had not voided or cancelled it. Even if an insurer cancels or avoids a policy due to some breach or misrepresentation, the insurer cannot use that cancellation as a reason to escape paying a third party who was injured. It ensures that innocent accident victims are not left without compensation simply because of disputes between the insurer and the vehicle owner.
real_world_examples: A truck owner in Mumbai obtains a motor insurance policy by concealing that the truck was used for carrying hazardous chemicals. After an accident injuring a pedestrian, the insurer discovers the misrepresentation and cancels the policy. Under Section 149, the insurer must still pay the injured pedestrian because the third-party liability was 'covered by the terms of the policy' at the time of the accident, even though the policy was subsequently cancelled.

A car owner in Delhi allows an unlicensed friend to drive, which breaches a policy condition. After a road accident injures a bystander, the insurer tries to avoid paying. The insurer must pay the injured third party under Section 149 because the liability would have been covered but for the breach condition, and can later recover the amount from the car owner.

An autorickshaw operator in Chennai does not disclose a prior accident history when obtaining insurance. The insurer avoids the policy on grounds of material non-disclosure after a collision injures a passenger. The Claims Tribunal in Chennai directs the insurer to pay the award to the victim because the liability falls within 'liability covered by the terms of the policy,' with the insurer retaining the right to recover from the owner.

A private bus operator in Hyderabad uses the vehicle for hire or reward without a permit, breaching a policy condition. After a serious road accident, the insurer seeks to deny liability citing the breach. The court holds that since the liability would have been covered under the original policy terms but for the breach, the insurer must pay the victims and then seek reimbursement from the operator.

A two-wheeler owner in Pune obtains insurance but later the insurer cancels the policy due to non-payment of premium installment. If the two-wheeler causes injury to a third party during the period when the policy was ostensibly valid, the court may hold that the liability was covered by the terms of the policy at the relevant time, compelling the insurer to satisfy the judgment.

Situations where the insurer has cancelled the policy due to a breach of a specified condition (such as unlicensed driving or use without permit), but a third party has already obtained a judgment or award against the insured person.
Third-party claims adjudicated by Claims Tribunals or courts in India where the insurer was given prior notice of proceedings under Section 149(2).
what_it_excludes: Liabilities arising from risks or uses that were never within the scope of the policy's coverage under any circumstances, such as deliberate criminal acts falling entirely outside the policy's terms.
Claims by the insured person against themselves or purely first-party losses not involving a third-party liability component under Section 147.

Liabilities where the insurer successfully establishes a valid defence under Section 149(2), such as use of the vehicle for organised racing, which is a specified excludable condition, and the liability was never covered even notionally.

Liabilities under policies that were void ab initio due to reasons entirely outside the scope of the motor insurance framework, such as a forged policy document that was never a real contract of insurance.

definitions.definition: "licence" means a driving licence or a learner's licence, as the context may require, issued by a competent authority under Chapter II of this Act authorising the person specified therein to drive a motor vehicle or a motor vehicle of any specified class or description, whether as a learner or otherwise.
definitions.plain_english: A 'licence' under the Motor Vehicles Act is the official government-issued document that permits a person to legally drive a motor vehicle on Indian roads. It can refer to either a full driving licence or a learner's licence depending on the situation. Without this document, a person is not legally allowed to operate any motor vehicle.
real_world_examples: A resident of Mumbai applies at the Regional Transport Office and receives a driving licence authorising him to drive a light motor vehicle — this document is his 'licence' under the Act.
A traffic police officer in Delhi stops a two-wheeler rider and demands to see her 'licence' under Section 130; the rider produces her driving licence issued by the competent authority in Bengaluru.
A learner in Hyderabad has been issued a learner's licence permitting her to drive a motor car under supervision — this learner's licence is also a 'licence' for the purposes of the Act.
Under Section 206, a police officer can seize and detain a vehicle if the driver fails to produce a valid 'licence', covering both full and learner's licences.

During enforcement under Section 217A, an officer checks whether a commercial truck driver holds a valid 'licence' authorising him to drive a heavy goods vehicle, as driving without one triggers penalties.

A person holding an effective driving licence issued by a reciprocating country who is temporarily in India — the term 'licence' in the Act's context helps determine whether such a person is 'duly licensed' to drive.
what_it_covers: A full driving licence issued by a competent licensing authority under Chapter II authorising the holder to drive a specified class of motor vehicle.
A learner's licence issued under Chapter II permitting a person to drive as a learner under prescribed conditions.
A driving licence authorising the holder to drive a specific category of vehicle such as a heavy goods vehicle, transport vehicle, or light motor vehicle.
A driving licence issued by an authority of a reciprocating country that is treated as effective under the Act.
A renewed or updated driving licence issued after the expiry of a prior licence under Chapter II provisions.
what_it_excludes: A conductor's licence issued under Chapter III, which authorises a person to act as a conductor of a stage carriage — not a 'licence' in the driving sense under Sections 206 and 217A.
A permit issued under Chapter V authorising the use or operation of a transport vehicle on specified routes — a permit is distinct from a licence.
A certificate of fitness issued for a motor vehicle under Chapter IV, which relates to the roadworthiness of the vehicle rather than the authorisation of the driver.
An authorisation or registration certificate for a dealer or manufacturer, which does not constitute a licence to drive.
An informal or unofficial document purporting to grant driving permission that has not been issued by a competent authority under Chapter II.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person holds a valid 'licence' is decisive in determining liability under Sections 206 and 217A — an officer may seize a vehicle or prosecute a driver for driving without a licence, and an insurer may repudiate a third-party insurance claim if the driver lacked a valid licence at the time of the accident. The presence or absence of a licence also determines whether a person is 'duly licensed' under the Act, affecting both criminal culpability and civil compensation obligations.

definitions.definition: 'Licensing authority' means an authority empowered to issue licences under Chapter II or, as the case may be, Chapter III of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988.
definitions.plain_english: A licensing authority is the official government body or officer designated to issue driving licences and conductor's licences in a given area. For driving licences, this is typically the Regional Transport Office (RTO) or a designated officer under Chapter II of the Motor Vehicles Act. For conductor's licences, it is the authority designated under Chapter III of the same Act.
real_world_examples: An applicant in Mumbai visits the Regional Transport Office (RTO) at Tardeo to apply for a permanent driving licence after completing the learner's licence period — the RTO officer acting as the licensing authority processes and issues the licence under Chapter II.

A person applying to work as a conductor on a KSRTC (Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation) bus approaches the designated officer at the district transport office in Bengaluru, who, acting as the licensing authority under Chapter III, issues the conductor's licence.

When a driving licence is suspended by court order for drunk driving in Delhi, the licensing authority (Delhi Transport Authority officer) is notified and records the endorsement of disqualification on the licence register.

A truck driver from Rajasthan wishes to upgrade his light motor vehicle licence to a heavy goods vehicle licence; he applies before the licensing authority at the RTO in Jaipur, which tests and grants the upgraded driving licence under Chapter II.

A teenager caught driving without a licence in Pune is brought before the magistrate, whose order is served on the licensing authority so that any future licence application by that individual can be flagged or conditions imposed.

The authority empowered to issue conductor's licences under Chapter III of the Motor Vehicles Act.
An officer or body notified by the State Government within a specified area as having the power to grant, renew, suspend, or revoke driving or conductor's licences.
Authority responsible for maintaining licence records, receiving endorsements, and processing disqualification orders related to driving and conductor licences.
what_it_excludes: The registering authority, which is a separate body empowered to register motor vehicles under Chapter IV and does not issue driving or conductor's licences.
Courts or magistrates who may order disqualification but are not themselves empowered to issue licences under Chapter II or III.
The State Transport Authority or Regional Transport Authority, which deal with permits for transport vehicles rather than the grant of individual driving or conductor's licences.
Police officers, even though they enforce traffic and licensing laws, as they are not empowered to issue licences under Chapter II or Chapter III.
Central Government bodies that may set rules but do not themselves act as licensing authorities for individual licence issuance under the Act.

definitions.definition: 'Light motor vehicle' means a transport vehicle or omnibus the gross vehicle weight of either of which, or a motor car or tractor or road-roller the unladen weight of any of which, does not exceed 7500 kilograms.
definitions.plain_english: A light motor vehicle is any smaller-sized vehicle — such as a car, small bus, tractor, or road-roller — whose weight (loaded or unloaded, depending on the type) does not go beyond 7500 kilograms. For transport vehicles and omnibuses, the total weight including load is measured, while for motor cars, tractors, and road-rollers, only the vehicle's own weight without any load is considered. Essentially, it covers everyday private cars, mini-buses, and small commercial vehicles that fall below this weight threshold.
real_world_examples: A Maruti Suzuki Swift or Hyundai Creta used for personal commuting in Delhi qualifies as a light motor vehicle because its unladen weight is well below 7500 kilograms, and the driver requires an LMV driving licence.

A Tata Ace mini-truck used by a small trader in Mumbai to deliver goods, with a gross vehicle weight under 7500 kilograms, is classified as a light motor vehicle and requires an LMV transport vehicle endorsement on the driving licence.

A school van or a 12-seater minibus operating as a contract carriage in Bengaluru, with a gross vehicle weight not exceeding 7500 kilograms, is a light motor vehicle for the purpose of registering and licensing under the Motor Vehicles Act.

A small road-roller with an unladen weight of 4000 kilograms used on a municipal road repair project in Chennai falls within the light motor vehicle category, requiring appropriate LMV registration and permits.

A farmer's tractor in Punjab with an unladen weight of 3500 kilograms towing a trailer on a state highway is considered a light motor vehicle, and the driver must hold a valid LMV licence to legally operate it on public roads.
what_it_covers: A private motor car (e.g., sedan or SUV) whose unladen weight does not exceed 7500 kilograms.
A transport vehicle or omnibus (e.g., small minibus or mini-truck) whose gross vehicle weight does not exceed 7500 kilograms.
A tractor or road-roller whose unladen weight does not exceed 7500 kilograms.
A maxicab or motorcab with a gross vehicle weight under 7500 kilograms used for hire or reward.
A small goods-carrying vehicle (e.g., Tata Ace, Mahindra Bolero pickup) with gross vehicle weight within the 7500 kg limit.
what_it_excludes: Heavy goods vehicles whose gross vehicle weight exceeds 12,000 kilograms, as they fall under a separate and higher classification.
Heavy passenger motor vehicles such as large buses or coaches whose gross vehicle weight exceeds 12,000 kilograms.
Medium goods vehicles and medium passenger motor vehicles that exceed the 7500 kg limit but fall below the heavy vehicle threshold of 12,000 kilograms.
Motor cycles, which are a distinct category of motor vehicle not included within the light motor vehicle definition.
Invalid carriages, which are specially designed vehicles for persons with disabilities and are governed by their own separate definition.
definitions.why_it_matters: Classification as a light motor vehicle determines the category of driving licence required under Chapter II (Sections 7, 8, and 10), meaning a person holding only an LMV licence is legally authorised to drive such vehicles but not heavier categories. It also governs applicable registration fees, permit requirements, insurance obligations, and road tax slabs, and has been the subject of significant Supreme Court litigation regarding whether an LMV licence holder can drive a transport vehicle falling within the LMV weight limit.

definitions.definition: A liquidator, as used in Section 151 of the Motor Vehicles Act, refers to a person duly appointed to wind up the affairs of a company that is undergoing compulsory or voluntary winding up, who is obligated to provide information to any person claiming that the company bears a liability covered under the insurance provisions of Chapter XI of the Act, and to allow inspection of relevant insurance contracts and documents.
definitions.plain_english: A liquidator is the official person appointed to close down a company and settle its debts and obligations when it is being wound up. Under the Motor Vehicles Act, if a company is being wound up and someone was injured in a motor accident caused by that company, the liquidator must tell that injured person whether the company had valid motor insurance. This ensures accident victims can still find out about and claim against any insurance policy the company held.
real_world_examples: A transport company operating trucks in Maharashtra is ordered to be wound up by the National Company Law Tribunal; a person injured in a road accident caused by one of its trucks approaches the liquidator appointed by the court to find out if the company held a valid insurance policy at the time of the accident, and the liquidator is legally bound to provide that information.

A private bus company in Tamil Nadu passes a resolution for voluntary winding up after financial collapse; a passenger injured in a bus accident before the winding up contacts the liquidator to check whether a certificate of insurance was in force, and the liquidator must allow the claimant to inspect and take copies of all relevant insurance documents.

A goods carriage company in Delhi is placed in liquidation and a pedestrian who was struck by one of its vehicles seeks to invoke Section 150 rights; the liquidator is obligated under Section 151 to disclose policy details and permit inspection of premium receipts and insurance contracts held by the company.

An e-commerce logistics company in Bengaluru undergoing court-ordered winding up has a pending motor accident claim; the liquidator appointed by the High Court must respond to the claimant's demand for information about the company's motor vehicle insurance policy, including particulars stated in the certificate of insurance.

A tourist vehicle operator company in Rajasthan being voluntarily wound up had a road accident involving foreign tourists before liquidation commenced; the liquidator must furnish insurance particulars to the tourists' legal representatives who are pursuing compensation under the Motor Vehicles Act.
what_it_covers: A liquidator appointed by a court in a compulsory winding up of a company that owned or operated motor vehicles involved in an accident.
A liquidator in a voluntary winding up who holds or has access to the company's motor insurance contracts, premium receipts, and certificates of insurance.
A liquidator who is obligated to disclose whether the wound-up company was insured or would have been insured under Chapter XI at the time a relevant motor accident occurred.
A liquidator required to allow a third-party claimant to inspect all insurance-related documents and obtain copies thereof for the purpose of enforcing rights under Section 150.
what_it_excludes: An official receiver or receiver appointed in individual insolvency proceedings, who is separately named in Section 151 and is not the same as a liquidator appointed for company winding up.
A personal representative of a deceased debtor or trustee in insolvency, who are distinct categories of persons also mentioned in Section 151 with their own obligations.
A manager or receiver appointed by debenture holders secured by a floating charge, who is separately categorised in Section 151 and does not fall under the specific role of liquidator.
A director or officer of the company who continues to act after winding up has commenced but has not been formally appointed as liquidator by a competent authority.
definitions.why_it_matters: If a liquidator refuses or fails to provide the required insurance information or denies inspection of relevant documents, they breach a statutory duty under Section 151, potentially obstructing a claimant's ability to enforce rights transferred under Section 150 against the insurer. This obligation ensures that the winding up of a company does not extinguish an accident victim's right to identify and claim against the motor insurer, making the liquidator a critical gatekeeper in the compensation process.

definitions.definition: 'Local authority' means a municipal committee, district board, body of port commissioners or other authority legally entitled to, or entrusted by the Government with, the control or management of a municipal or local fund.
definitions.plain_english: A local authority is any officially recognised government body at the city, town, district, or port level that is responsible for managing local public funds and civic affairs. This includes municipal corporations, panchayats, cantonment boards, and port trusts. These bodies have legal standing to exercise powers and responsibilities within a defined geographic area.
real_world_examples: The Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) acting as a local authority under the MV Act when designating parking places and regulating traffic flow on city roads under Section 117.
The Chennai Port Trust functioning as a local authority when managing vehicle movement and parking within port premises, engaging with the provisions of the Act.
A District Panchayat in rural Rajasthan being recognised as a local authority for purposes of enforcing compulsory insurance requirements under Section 146 within its jurisdiction.
The Delhi Municipal Corporation issuing directions for vehicle parking zones and stand locations on public roads in exercise of its powers as a local authority under Section 117.
The Kolkata Municipal Corporation coordinating with transport authorities under the MV Act to designate and regulate stage carriage stands and halting points within municipal limits.
what_it_covers: Municipal corporations and municipalities such as the Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation or Pune Municipal Corporation managing local civic affairs.
District boards or zila parishads legally entrusted by the State Government with management of district-level local funds.
Port trust bodies such as the Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust (JNPT) that are legally entitled to manage port area funds and infrastructure.
Cantonment boards established under the Cantonments Act that exercise local governance powers within cantonment areas.
Town panchayats or gram panchayats entrusted by the Government with control over a local fund within their territorial jurisdiction.
what_it_excludes: Central Government ministries or departments, which are not local or municipal in character and do not manage a local fund.
State Government departments such as the Public Works Department (PWD), which are arms of the State rather than independent local authorities.
Private bodies, companies, or NGOs that may manage public infrastructure under contract but are not legally entrusted with control of a municipal or local fund.
Statutory regulatory bodies such as the Regional Transport Authority (RTA) or State Transport Authority, which are transport-specific and not local governance bodies.
Individual government officers or officials acting in personal capacity, as opposed to a collegial or institutional local body.
definitions.why_it_matters: Under Section 117 of the MV Act, local authorities are empowered to designate parking places and stands for motor vehicles, making their identity critical for the valid exercise of that regulatory power. Under Section 146, the compulsory insurance requirements and their enforcement interact with notifications and directions issued by local authorities, meaning that whether a body qualifies as a 'local authority' determines the legal validity of such directions and the consequent obligations on vehicle owners and operators.

definitions.definition: A road designated as a 'main road' by the State Government or any authority authorised by it, either by notification in the Official Gazette or by the erection of the appropriate traffic sign referred to in Part A of the Schedule, for the purposes of the driving regulations made by the Central Government under the Motor Vehicles Act.
definitions.plain_english: A 'main road' is a road that has been officially designated as such by the State Government, either through a formal government notification or by putting up specific traffic signs at suitable places. This designation is important because it determines which driving rules — set by the Central Government — apply on that road. Think of it as the government officially labelling certain roads as priority or primary roads for traffic regulation purposes.
real_world_examples: The Maharashtra State Government issues a notification in the Official Gazette designating NH-48 (Mumbai-Pune Expressway service roads) and certain State Highways within Pune city limits as 'main roads', making Central Government driving regulations relating to right-of-way at intersections specifically applicable on those stretches.

In Delhi, the Delhi Transport Authority erects 'main road' traffic signs (as specified in Part A of the Schedule) at the entry points of Ring Road and Outer Ring Road, thereby designating them as main roads so that vehicles on these roads have priority over vehicles entering from side streets under the driving regulations.

The Tamil Nadu government, by a Gazette notification, designates Anna Salai (Mount Road) in Chennai as a main road, enabling traffic enforcement authorities to strictly enforce Central Government driving regulations regarding lane discipline, overtaking restrictions, and right-of-way obligations specific to main roads.

In Bengaluru, the Karnataka government designates MG Road and Brigade Road as main roads by erecting appropriate Part A Schedule traffic signs, so that motorists on adjoining smaller roads are required under driving regulations to give way to vehicles travelling on these designated main roads.

During a road safety audit in Jaipur, the Rajasthan State Government re-designates certain urban arterial roads like Tonk Road and Ajmer Road as main roads via Official Gazette notification, triggering the application of specific Central Government driving regulations regarding speed limits, overtaking, and intersection priority for those corridors.
what_it_covers: Roads designated by the State Government through a notification published in the Official Gazette specifically for purposes of Central Government driving regulations.
Roads on which the appropriate traffic sign from Part A of the Schedule has been erected at suitable places by the State Government or an authorised authority to indicate 'main road' status.
State Highways, National Highway service roads, and major urban arterial roads formally designated as main roads to regulate traffic priority and driving conduct at intersections.

Any road, whether urban or rural, that has received the formal 'main road' designation, making Central Government driving regulations — such as right-of-way rules — applicable to traffic on that road.
what_it_excludes: Roads that have not been formally designated by a Gazette notification or by erection of a Part A Schedule traffic sign, regardless of how busy or wide they are in practice.
Village roads, rural link roads, internal colony roads, and private roads that have never been notified or sign-posted as main roads under Section 116.
Roads designated for other specific purposes under the Act (such as notified routes or inter-State routes) but not separately notified as main roads under Section 116.
Temporary or ad hoc road designations made without the prescribed procedure of Gazette notification or appropriate traffic sign erection under this section.
definitions.why_it_matters: The designation of a road as a 'main road' directly determines which Central Government driving regulations apply on it, particularly rules relating to right-of-way at intersections where a main road meets a lesser road — failure to comply with these regulations on a designated main road can result in prosecution for traffic offences. Additionally, the presence or absence of this designation affects the legal obligations of drivers at junctions and the validity of traffic signs erected under Section 116.

definitions.definition: A traffic sign included in Part A of the Schedule, or any traffic sign of similar form (that is to say, consisting of or including a circular disc displaying a device, word or figure and having a red ground or border) placed or erected for the purpose of regulating motor vehicle traffic under sub-section (1) of section 116.
definitions.plain_english: A mandatory traffic sign is an official road sign that drivers must strictly obey by law. These signs are typically circular with a red border or red background and display a symbol, word, or number that either prohibits or requires a specific action from the driver. Examples include stop signs, no-entry signs, and speed limit prohibition signs. Unlike informational or warning signs, ignoring a mandatory traffic sign is a direct legal offence.
real_world_examples: A 'No Entry' circular sign with a red border at the entrance of a one-way street in Connaught Place, New Delhi — a driver who enters that street in violation is disobeying a mandatory traffic sign.
A round 'Speed Limit 40 km/h' sign with a red border on a Mumbai highway service road — a truck driver exceeding this speed is in breach of his duty under Section 119.
A 'Stop' sign placed at an unmanned railway level crossing in rural Rajasthan — a bus driver failing to halt before the crossing is violating the mandatory traffic sign obligation.
A 'No Overtaking' circular disc with red border on a two-lane highway in Punjab — a car driver who overtakes at that stretch is in contravention of Section 119.

A 'Compulsory Turn Left' circular sign at a busy intersection in Bengaluru — a motorcyclist going straight through instead of turning left is disobeying a mandatory traffic sign placed under Section 116(1).
what_it_covers: All traffic signs listed in Part A of the Schedule to the Motor Vehicles Act, which include prohibitory and mandatory signs such as 'No Entry', 'Stop', 'No Overtaking', and compulsory turn signs.
Any circular disc-shaped sign displaying a device, word, or figure with a red ground or red border, placed or erected by a competent authority under Section 116(1) to regulate motor vehicle traffic.

Signs erected by Central or State authorities on public roads specifically for the purpose of regulating motor vehicle movement, regardless of whether they are listed in Part A, provided they conform to the circular red-border form.
A 'Compulsory Ahead Only' sign placed at a road junction by a Municipal Corporation under delegated authority under Section 116(1), since it matches the prescribed form.
what_it_excludes: Warning signs (typically triangular with a red border) such as 'Dangerous Dip' or 'School Ahead', which alert drivers to hazards but do not impose a mandatory obligation — these fall outside Part A of the Schedule.
Informatory or directional signs (typically rectangular or square) such as route markers, distance boards, or service facility signs, which provide information but do not regulate conduct.
Hand signals or verbal directions given by a police officer, which are separately covered under Section 119 but are not 'traffic signs' within this definition.
Temporary barriers, cones, or unofficial signs placed by private parties without authority under Section 116(1), even if they resemble the circular red-border form.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a sign qualifies as a 'mandatory traffic sign' determines whether a driver's non-compliance constitutes a punishable offence under Section 119 of the Motor Vehicles Act, attracting penalties for failure to obey traffic signs. If a sign does not meet this definition, a driver cannot be held liable under Section 119 for disregarding it, making the classification critical for both prosecution and defence in traffic violation cases.

definitions.definition: 'manufacturer' means a person who is engaged in the manufacture of motor vehicles.
definitions.plain_english: A manufacturer is any person or company that is in the business of making motor vehicles. This includes companies that build cars, trucks, buses, motorcycles, or any other motorised vehicle meant to be used on roads. The term covers the entire act of producing or assembling a motor vehicle from components.
real_world_examples: Maruti Suzuki India Limited, which produces passenger cars like the Swift and Baleno at its Gurugram and Manesar plants, qualifies as a manufacturer under the Motor Vehicles Act.
Tata Motors Limited, which manufactures heavy commercial vehicles, buses, and passenger cars across its factories in Pune and Jamshedpur, is a manufacturer under this Act.
Hero MotoCorp, which assembles and produces two-wheeled motor vehicles such as motorcycles and scooters at its Dharuhera plant, is considered a manufacturer for the purposes of this Act.
Ashok Leyland, which fabricates heavy goods vehicles and public service vehicles (buses) at its Chennai facility, falls within the definition of manufacturer under the Act.
A newly incorporated Indian electric vehicle company like Ola Electric, which manufactures e-scooters at its factory in Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu, is also covered by this definition.

Force Motors Limited, which produces light commercial vehicles and multi-utility vehicles in Pune, is classified as a manufacturer and bears obligations under Chapter related to vehicle standards and type approval.
what_it_covers: Large automobile companies such as Maruti Suzuki, Tata Motors, or Mahindra & Mahindra that produce four-wheeled motor vehicles on a commercial scale.
Two-wheeler manufacturers such as Bajaj Auto or TVS Motor Company that assemble motorcycles and scooters intended for use on public roads.
Commercial vehicle producers such as Ashok Leyland or VECV that manufacture buses, trucks, and heavy goods vehicles.
Electric vehicle manufacturers producing e-rickshaws, e-carts, or electric two-wheelers intended for road use.
Any person or entity that assembles complete motor vehicles from imported or domestically sourced components as part of their business activity.
what_it_excludes: Dealers who only sell, repair, or build bodies onto existing chassis but do not engage in the manufacture of the motor vehicle itself.
Importers who procure fully manufactured motor vehicles from foreign manufacturers and distribute them in India without engaging in any manufacturing activity.
Owners or individuals who privately modify or alter their own vehicles for personal use, as they are not 'engaged in the manufacture' of motor vehicles as a business.
Spare parts or component manufacturers (e.g., tyre companies, engine parts suppliers) who produce parts but do not manufacture complete motor vehicles.
Transport companies or fleet operators who own and operate motor vehicles but have no role in their production or assembly.
definitions.why_it_matters: The identification of a 'manufacturer' triggers specific obligations under the Act, particularly under Section 109, which empowers authorities to hold manufacturers accountable for compliance with construction, equipment, and safety standards prescribed for motor vehicles. Whether an entity qualifies as a manufacturer determines its liability for defective vehicle design or non-compliance with type approval norms, and failure to meet these standards can result in penalties, recall orders, or prohibition of sale of non-compliant vehicles.

definitions.definition: A fact of such a nature as to influence the judgment of a prudent insurer in determining whether he will take the risk and, if so, at what premium and on what conditions.
definitions.plain_english: A 'material fact' in motor vehicle insurance is any piece of information that would affect an insurance company's decision about whether to provide coverage, how much to charge for it, or what conditions to attach. If you hide or misrepresent such a fact when getting your policy, the insurer can potentially avoid paying claims. It is essentially any detail that a careful, reasonable insurer would consider important before agreeing to insure a vehicle.
real_world_examples: A vehicle owner in Mumbai fails to disclose to the insurer that the car has been significantly modified with a high-performance turbo engine, which increases the risk profile of the vehicle. This undisclosed modification is a material fact that could affect the insurer's premium calculation.

A truck owner in Delhi applies for a commercial vehicle insurance policy but does not reveal that the truck was previously involved in a major accident and had its chassis repaired. The prior damage history constitutes a material fact that a prudent insurer would consider before setting premiums.

A taxi operator in Chennai obtains insurance without disclosing that the vehicle is used as a contract carriage operating on night routes, instead representing it as a private vehicle. The actual commercial use is a material fact influencing risk assessment.

A bus operator in Kolkata fails to inform the insurer that the designated driver has a history of traffic violations and licence disqualification. The driver's poor record is a material fact relevant to the insurer's decision to cover or exclude that driver.

A goods vehicle owner in Pune does not disclose that the vehicle routinely carries hazardous chemicals beyond the permitted weight limits. This operational detail constitutes a material fact that would influence the insurer's terms and premium.
what_it_covers: Prior accident history of the insured vehicle that was concealed at the time of obtaining the policy.
Undisclosed modification or alteration to the vehicle that changes its risk category or performance specifications.
Concealment of the vehicle's actual commercial use (e.g., running it as a taxi when insured as a private car).
Non-disclosure of the principal driver's past disqualifications or repeated traffic offences.
Failure to reveal that the vehicle is used to carry dangerous or hazardous goods beyond its permitted capacity.
what_it_excludes: Facts that are trivial or routine and would not influence a prudent insurer's decision on coverage, premium, or conditions.
Information already publicly known or recorded in official registers that the insurer is presumed to have access to independently.
Minor cosmetic changes to the vehicle that do not affect its risk profile or the insurer's assessment of liability.
Facts that the insurer expressly waived the right to be informed about or chose not to inquire into during the policy application process.
Irrelevant personal details of the owner that have no bearing on the vehicle's use, operation, or accident risk.
definitions.why_it_matters: If a motor vehicle insurance policy is found to have been obtained by non-disclosure of a material fact or by a materially false representation, the insurer is entitled under Section 149(2)(b) to defend against paying a third-party claim on that ground, potentially voiding the policy; this definition therefore determines whether a third-party accident victim can recover compensation from the insurer or is left to pursue only the individual tortfeasor.

definitions.definition: A 'material particular' refers to any specific detail, fact, or information furnished in connection with the registration of a motor vehicle or a policy of insurance that is of such significance that, if false or misrepresented, would have influenced the decision of the registering authority to grant registration or the insurer to issue the policy. It includes details such as the engine number, chassis number, identity of the owner, nature and use of the vehicle, or any other particulars recorded in the certificate of registration or policy documents.
definitions.plain_english: A 'material particular' is any important piece of information provided when registering a vehicle or obtaining insurance that could affect the outcome of that process. If someone gives false information on any such key detail — like the engine number, the owner's name, or how the vehicle is used — it is considered a misrepresentation of a material particular. Such false information can lead to cancellation of the vehicle's registration or the insurance policy being voided.
real_world_examples: A vehicle owner in Delhi submits a registration application stating the chassis number as 'MH1234' but the actual chassis number embossed on the vehicle is 'MH5678'. This incorrect chassis number is a false material particular, and the RTO can cancel the registration under Section 55.

A truck owner in Mumbai obtains a commercial vehicle registration by falsely declaring that the vehicle will be used for private purposes to avoid higher fees, whereas it is actually used for hire or reward. The declared use is a material particular, and misrepresenting it renders the registration liable to cancellation.

An insurer in Pune discovers that the vehicle owner declared the vehicle's seating capacity as 6 in the insurance proposal form, whereas the registered capacity is 12. Since seating capacity is a material particular affecting premium and liability, the insurer can use this as a defence under Section 149 to resist paying a third-party claim.

A vehicle dealer in Chennai assists a buyer in registering a vehicle using forged documents that show a different engine number than the actual one. The engine number is a material particular, and the fraudulent registration obtained on this basis can be cancelled by the registering authority after notice to the owner.

An owner in Kolkata applies for registration of a vehicle under a particular owner's name to avail a benefit, when the actual owner is a company. The identity of the owner is a material particular, and misrepresentation can lead to cancellation of registration and potential legal proceedings.
what_it_covers: Engine number or chassis number declared in the certificate of registration that differs from the number actually embossed on the vehicle.
The name, identity, or address of the registered owner as submitted at the time of registration, if found to be false.
The declared nature of use or class of the vehicle (e.g., private versus commercial) recorded in registration documents, if misrepresented.
Details of the vehicle such as seating capacity, unladen weight, or fuel type provided in insurance or registration documents that affect coverage or fee calculation.
Representations about the origin, ownership history, or encumbrances on the vehicle made in documents supporting the registration application.
what_it_excludes: Minor clerical or typographical errors in registration documents that do not affect the substance of the registration or the identity of the vehicle or owner.
Information that is irrelevant or immaterial to the decision to grant registration or issue a policy, such as the colour preference of the owner or optional accessories.

Subsequent changes in facts after registration has been lawfully obtained, such as a change in the owner's address not updated with the RTO, which do not retroactively render the original registration false.
Technical non-compliance with procedural requirements that do not involve a false statement of fact, such as submitting a form in the wrong format.
Conditions or events that occur after the issuance of the certificate of registration that were not misrepresented at the time of application.
definitions.why_it_matters: A finding that registration was obtained on the basis of a false material particular empowers the registering authority under Section 55 to cancel the vehicle's registration, rendering the vehicle unlawful to operate on public roads. Under Section 149, an insurer may defend a third-party claim by establishing that the policy is void because it was obtained through misrepresentation of a material particular, potentially relieving the insurer of its obligation to satisfy the judgment or award in favour of the accident victim.

definitions.definition: "Maxicab" means any motor vehicle constructed or adapted to carry more than six passengers, but not more than twelve passengers, excluding the driver, for hire or reward.
definitions.plain_english: A maxicab is a paid passenger vehicle that can seat between 7 and 12 passengers, not counting the driver. It is used to transport people for a fee, making it a commercial vehicle. Common examples include large taxis or shared cabs that carry more passengers than a regular cab but fewer than a full-sized bus.
real_world_examples: A Tempo Traveller operating as a shared taxi between Delhi and Meerut, carrying 10 passengers who each pay a fixed fare, qualifies as a maxicab.
A Mahindra Force van adapted to seat 8 passengers and used by a tour operator in Goa to ferry tourists to beaches for hire qualifies as a maxicab.
A 12-seater Sumo or Innova Crysta (modified) operating on a fixed route between two towns in Himachal Pradesh on a contract carriage permit is classified as a maxicab.
An operator in Mumbai running a shared cab service using a 10-passenger van for corporate employee transportation on a hire basis is operating a maxicab under the Motor Vehicles Act.
A vehicle plying as an app-based shared mobility service in Bengaluru with seating capacity for 9 passengers and charging per-seat fares falls within the maxicab definition.
what_it_covers: A Tempo Traveller or Force Traveller carrying 7 to 12 fare-paying passengers on a contract or shared basis.
Any motor vehicle specifically constructed or factory-adapted with seating for 7 to 12 passengers (excluding driver) and operated for hire or reward.
A maxicab included within the definition of 'contract carriage' under Section 2 of the Motor Vehicles Act, even if separate fares are charged to individual passengers.
A 10-seater van rented by a travel agency to transport tourists for a fixed fee, where the vehicle seats fall within the 7–12 passenger range.
what_it_excludes: A motorcab or regular taxi carrying not more than six passengers excluding the driver — such vehicles fall under the definition of 'motorcab', not maxicab.
An omnibus or stage carriage carrying more than twelve passengers excluding the driver, which falls under a different vehicle classification entirely.
Private vehicles carrying 7–12 passengers without any element of hire or reward — the commercial purpose (hire or reward) is an essential requirement for the maxicab definition.
Educational institution buses carrying students, which are separately defined and classified as 'educational institution bus' regardless of seating capacity.
Goods carriages adapted to carry workers or crew without being engaged in passenger transport for hire or reward.

definitions.definition: The maximum speed means the upper speed limit fixed for a motor vehicle or class or description of motor vehicles under the Motor Vehicles Act or by or under any other law for the time being in force, as may be notified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette, beyond which no person shall drive or cause or allow a motor vehicle to be driven in any public place; such maximum speed may further be restricted by the State Government or any authority authorised by it for reasons of public safety, road conditions, or the nature of a bridge, either generally or for a particular area or road.
definitions.plain_english: Maximum speed is the highest speed at which a motor vehicle is legally allowed to travel on a public road in India. This limit is set by the Central Government and can be further lowered by the State Government for specific roads, areas, or types of vehicles. Driving faster than this limit is a punishable offence under the Motor Vehicles Act.
real_world_examples: On a National Highway in India, the Central Government notification fixes the maximum speed for a private car at 120 km/h; a driver caught doing 140 km/h on NH-48 (Delhi–Mumbai corridor) is liable for speeding.

The Maharashtra Government, by notification, restricts the maximum speed on the Bandra-Worli Sea Link to 80 km/h due to the nature of the elevated bridge structure; a motorist driving at 100 km/h there violates section 112.

A State Road Transport Corporation bus operating on a hilly route in Himachal Pradesh is subject to a State Government-imposed maximum speed of 40 km/h on ghat sections, and the driver must not exceed this even if the Central Government limit for heavy passenger vehicles is higher.

During a public festival in Bengaluru, the city traffic police authority notifies a maximum speed of 30 km/h in a particular congested area for one month; vehicles including auto-rickshaws and cars must comply with this temporary restriction.

A goods vehicle carrying chemicals on an urban road in Delhi is subject to a lower maximum speed fixed by the State Government than that applicable on an expressway, and the driver exceeding this limit may be prosecuted under the Act.

An e-cart operating in a notified area of Varanasi is subject to the maximum speed fixed specifically for that class of vehicle by the Central Government notification, and exceeding it constitutes an offence even on roads with no visible speed sign.
what_it_covers: The highest permissible speed for any motor vehicle or class of motor vehicles notified by the Central Government for use on public roads.
Speed limits imposed by State Governments or authorised authorities on specific roads, bridges, or areas in the interest of public safety or road conditions.
Reduced maximum speeds applicable to motor vehicles towing a trailer, notified either generally or for a particular route or area.
Temporary maximum speed restrictions imposed by State authorities for up to one month without requiring a formal Official Gazette notification.
Class-specific maximum speeds for heavy goods vehicles, heavy passenger motor vehicles, motor cycles, and other categories of motor vehicles as notified.
what_it_excludes: Vehicles registered under section 60 of the Act while being used in the execution of military manoeuvres within the notified area and period under the Manoeuvres, Field Firing and Artillery Practice Act, 1938 — these are exempt from section 112.
Minimum speed limits, which are a separate concept governed by the same section but refer to the lowest permissible speed, not the upper ceiling.
Speed restrictions applicable on private property or non-public roads, as section 112 applies only in a 'public place'.

definitions.definition: 'medium goods vehicle' means any goods carriage other than a light motor vehicle or a heavy goods vehicle.
definitions.plain_english: A medium goods vehicle is any truck or goods-carrying vehicle that falls in the middle weight category — heavier than a light motor vehicle but not as heavy as a heavy goods vehicle. In practical terms, it covers goods carriers with a gross vehicle weight above 7,500 kilograms and up to 12,000 kilograms. These vehicles occupy the intermediate tier in the Motor Vehicles Act's classification of commercial freight vehicles.
real_world_examples: A Tata LPT 1109 truck used by a Delhi wholesale distributor to transport packaged goods between warehouses, with a gross vehicle weight of approximately 11,000 kg, qualifies as a medium goods vehicle.
A Mahindra Furio 7 cargo truck engaged in inter-city transportation of agricultural produce from Nashik to Mumbai markets, weighing around 8,500 kg GVW, falls under this category.
A medium-sized Ashok Leyland cargo truck used by an e-commerce logistics company in Bengaluru for last-mile bulk delivery with a GVW of 10,000 kg is classified as a medium goods vehicle.

A refrigerated van used by a cold chain logistics company in Punjab to transport dairy products between cities, with a GVW between 7,500 kg and 12,000 kg, is treated as a medium goods vehicle for licensing and permit purposes.
A construction company's flatbed truck in Hyderabad carrying steel rods with a GVW of 9,000 kg must be registered and operated under the regulatory framework applicable to medium goods vehicles.
what_it_covers: Any goods carriage with a gross vehicle weight exceeding 7,500 kg but not exceeding 12,000 kg.
A truck adapted solely for carrying goods that does not meet the unladen weight threshold for a heavy goods vehicle and exceeds the GVW limit of a light motor vehicle.
A vehicle not originally constructed for goods carriage but used for carriage of goods, provided its weight places it in the intermediate category between light and heavy goods vehicles.
Refrigerated trucks, flatbed lorries, and tipper trucks whose GVW falls within the medium range as defined by exclusion from the light and heavy categories.
what_it_excludes: Light motor vehicles — goods carriages with a gross vehicle weight of 7,500 kg or less are classified as light motor vehicles, not medium goods vehicles.
Heavy goods vehicles — any goods carriage with a gross vehicle weight exceeding 12,000 kg is classified as a heavy goods vehicle and is outside this definition.
Tractors and road-rollers, which are governed by separate weight thresholds under the definitions of light and heavy motor vehicles.
Passenger-carrying vehicles such as omnibuses, stage carriages, and contract carriages, even if they have some cargo capacity, as they are not 'goods carriages' under the Act.
Personal luggage carriers or trailers attached to private motor cars, which are excluded from the definition of 'goods carriage' under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Classification as a medium goods vehicle determines the category of driving licence required (transport vehicle endorsement with medium goods vehicle authorisation), the applicable permit conditions under the goods carriage permit framework, and the fitness certificate standards and fee structures prescribed by the registering authority. Misclassification can result in prosecution for driving without a valid licence, operating without a proper permit, and liability for enhanced penalties under the Motor Vehicles Act.

definitions.definition: 'Medium passenger motor vehicle' means any public service vehicle or private service vehicle, or educational institution bus other than a motor cycle, invalid carriage, light motor vehicle or heavy passenger motor vehicle.
definitions.plain_english: A medium passenger motor vehicle is a vehicle used to carry passengers — such as a bus or van operated for public use, private use, or by a school/college — that is neither too small (light motor vehicle) nor too large (heavy passenger motor vehicle). It falls in the middle weight and size category between light and heavy passenger vehicles. Motor cycles and invalid carriages are not included in this category.
real_world_examples: A 20-seater minibus operated by a private company in Pune to transport employees to and from an industrial estate qualifies as a medium passenger motor vehicle.
A school van owned by a private school in Delhi with a gross vehicle weight between 7,500 kg and 12,000 kg used to transport students falls under this category as an educational institution bus.

A tempo traveller (say, a 12-seater force traveller) used as a stage carriage on a rural route in Maharashtra with gross vehicle weight exceeding the light motor vehicle threshold would be classified as a medium passenger motor vehicle.

A privately operated shuttle service in Bengaluru running a midi-bus between residential areas and IT parks, with a gross vehicle weight above 7,500 kg but not exceeding 12,000 kg, is a medium passenger motor vehicle.

A pilgrimage transport van hired by a group of travellers in Varanasi for a fixed trip, with seating for 15 passengers and gross vehicle weight in the medium range, constitutes a medium passenger motor vehicle used as a contract carriage.
what_it_covers: A public service vehicle (such as a midi-bus or minibus) with gross vehicle weight above 7,500 kg but not exceeding 12,000 kg.
A private service vehicle used by a company to ferry employees, falling within the medium weight range between light and heavy passenger vehicles.
An educational institution bus owned by a school or college with gross vehicle weight exceeding the light motor vehicle limit but not exceeding 12,000 kg.
A contract carriage minibus operating in a city with seating capacity above what constitutes a maxicab but not heavy enough to qualify as a heavy passenger motor vehicle.
what_it_excludes: Light motor vehicles — any public service vehicle, private service vehicle, or educational institution bus with gross vehicle weight not exceeding 7,500 kg is excluded.
Heavy passenger motor vehicles — any public service vehicle, private service vehicle, or educational institution bus with gross vehicle weight exceeding 12,000 kg is excluded.
Motor cycles — two-wheeled motor vehicles are explicitly excluded from this definition even if used for passenger transport.
Invalid carriages — vehicles specially designed for persons with physical disabilities are explicitly excluded.
A motor car used privately by an individual, as it is neither a public service vehicle nor a private service vehicle in the statutory sense.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a vehicle as a 'medium passenger motor vehicle' directly determines the type of driving licence required under Chapter II and the permit category applicable under Chapter V of the Motor Vehicles Act, meaning a driver without the appropriate endorsement for this class commits an offence and the operator may face permit-related penalties. It also governs applicable fitness certificate standards, insurance requirements, and tax/fee structures under State motor vehicle taxation laws.

definitions.definition: A member of a State Transport Authority or Regional Transport Authority means any person (whether official or non-official) appointed by the State Government to constitute such Authority under Section 68, excluding any person who has any financial interest, whether as proprietor, employee or otherwise, in any transport undertaking; and in the case of a Regional Transport Authority, not more than two such other persons, and in the case of a State Transport Authority, not more than four such other persons, in addition to the Chairman.
definitions.plain_english: A 'member' is a person officially appointed by the State Government to sit on a State or Regional Transport Authority — a body that regulates road transport permits and related matters. These members can be government officials or private individuals, but they must not have any financial stake in any transport business. If a member later acquires such a financial interest, they must disclose it and resign from the Authority.
real_world_examples: A retired IAS officer from Maharashtra, with no ownership or employment interest in any bus company, is appointed by the State Government as a member of the Maharashtra State Transport Authority to help regulate stage carriage permits.

A senior advocate with appellate authority experience is appointed as a non-official member of the Regional Transport Authority for the Pune region to assist in deciding permit disputes for goods carriages.

An official of the District Collectorate in Rajasthan, whose government has a financial interest in a state transport undertaking, is appointed as a member of the Regional Transport Authority — this is permissible under the proviso because he is not directly connected with the management or operation of that transport undertaking.

A businessperson initially appointed as a member of the Delhi State Transport Authority later purchases shares in a private bus company; under Section 68, they are required to notify the State Government in writing within four weeks and vacate their office as member.

In the absence of the Chairman of the Regional Transport Authority in Tamil Nadu, one of the non-official members presides over a meeting and exercises the Chairman's functions, as expressly permitted by the proviso to Section 68(2).

The Himachal Pradesh Government, finding it impractical to appoint multiple members for a remote region, constitutes a single-member Regional Transport Authority consisting of a judicial officer, in accordance with the second proviso to Section 68(2).

A single official with judicial or appellate experience appointed as the sole member of a Regional Transport Authority where the State Government so decides under the second proviso to Section 68(2).
A member who is permitted to preside over Authority meetings in the absence of the Chairman, even without judicial or appellate experience, as allowed by the first proviso to Section 68(2).
what_it_excludes: A person who is a proprietor, employee, or otherwise holds a financial interest in any transport undertaking — such a person is expressly disqualified from being appointed or continuing as a member.

Officials directly connected with the management or operation of a government-owned transport undertaking, even if the government itself has a financial interest in that undertaking.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a 'member' determines the valid constitution of a State or Regional Transport Authority and hence the legality of all permits, directions, and decisions made by that Authority under Chapter V of the Motor Vehicles Act; an improperly constituted Authority due to a disqualified member could render its decisions — including grant or refusal of transport permits under Section 142 — legally vulnerable to challenge.

definitions.definition: Minimum speed means the lower threshold of speed fixed for a motor vehicle or any specified class or description of motor vehicles, below which no person shall drive or cause or allow such vehicle to be driven in any public place, as fixed under the Motor Vehicles Act or by or under any other law for the time being in force, or as notified by the State Government or any authority authorised by it in the interest of public safety, convenience, or on account of the nature of any road or bridge.
definitions.plain_english: Minimum speed is the slowest speed at which a vehicle must travel on a particular road or in a particular area, as set by the government. Driving too slowly below this limit is just as much a violation as driving too fast above the maximum speed limit. These limits are usually set on expressways or highways where very slow vehicles can cause traffic hazards or accidents.
real_world_examples: On the Delhi-Meerut Expressway, a minimum speed of 60 km/h is prescribed for certain lanes; a truck crawling at 30 km/h in such a lane would be in violation of the minimum speed limit under Section 112.

The National Highways Authority of India notifies minimum speed limits on access-controlled expressways like the Mumbai-Pune Expressway; a car driving at 40 km/h in the fast lane would be in breach of the prescribed minimum speed.

A State Government issues a notification fixing a minimum speed of 50 km/h on a particular State highway bypass; a tractor-trolley moving at 20 km/h on that stretch without exemption would attract liability under this provision.

On a designated lane of the Yamuna Expressway where a 80 km/h minimum is prescribed for heavy goods vehicles, a goods carriage travelling at 50 km/h would be violating the minimum speed requirement and the driver could be penalised.

During a road safety audit, traffic police on a national highway notice several private cars travelling well below the notified minimum speed, causing tailgating and rear-end collisions, and issue challans for violation of minimum speed under the Motor Vehicles Act.
what_it_covers: The lowest permissible speed set by the Central or State Government for motor vehicles on specified roads, highways, or expressways in India.
Minimum speed limits notified by an authorised authority for a particular class or description of motor vehicles, such as heavy goods vehicles or passenger buses, on a designated road or area.
Minimum speed limits applicable to motor vehicles towing a trailer on specific roads where slow movement poses a hazard to public safety.
Temporary minimum speed restrictions imposed without a formal gazette notification when the restriction is to remain in force for not more than one month.
what_it_excludes: Vehicles registered under Section 60 of the Act that are being used in the execution of military manoeuvres within the area and during the period specified under the Manoeuvres, Field Firing and Artillery Practice Act, 1938.
Maximum speed limits, which are separately governed and capped by Central Government notifications and are a distinct concept from minimum speed.

definitions.definition: "Motorcab" means any motor vehicle constructed or adapted to carry not more than six passengers excluding the driver for hire or reward.
definitions.plain_english: A motor cab is a small hired vehicle — like a taxi or auto-cab — that can carry up to six paying passengers (not counting the driver). It is built or modified specifically to transport people in exchange for money. Common examples include city taxis and app-based cab services operating small cars.
real_world_examples: An Ola or Uber sedan (e.g., Maruti Swift Dzire) operating in Mumbai picking up passengers for a fare is a classic motor cab, as it carries up to 4–5 passengers for hire or reward.
A traditional Kolkata yellow Ambassador taxi registered with the city's taxi association and charging metered fares qualifies as a motor cab under the MV Act.
A Mahindra e2o Plus electric cab operated by a city-level aggregator in Bengaluru carrying passengers for a fixed per-km charge is a motor cab.
A Rapido or Meru cab running in Delhi with a maximum seating of six passengers (excluding the driver) and charging customers per ride falls squarely within the motor cab definition.
A tourist cab in Goa — a Innova or similar vehicle adapted to carry six passengers — hired by a travel agency for sightseeing tours at agreed fares is a motor cab.
A shared auto-taxi in Chennai (four-wheeler) that is constructed to carry not more than six paying passengers and collects per-seat fares qualifies as a motor cab.
what_it_covers: Any motor car or vehicle constructed or adapted to carry a maximum of six passengers (excluding the driver) that charges fares for transportation.
App-based cab aggregator vehicles (e.g., Ola, Uber, Rapido cabs) operating small sedans or hatchbacks for hire or reward with not more than six passengers.
Traditional metered taxis in cities like Mumbai, Delhi, and Kolkata that carry up to six paying passengers.
A motor cab operating as a contract carriage even when separate fares are charged to individual passengers, as explicitly included in the definition of 'contract carriage' in Section 2.
Tourist taxis and hired vehicles adapted to carry not more than six passengers for a fixed or agreed rate.
what_it_excludes: Maxicabs, which are vehicles carrying more than six but not more than twelve passengers (excluding the driver) for hire or reward — these fall under a separate definition.
Stage carriages and omnibuses, which are designed to carry more than twelve passengers and stop at designated points to pick up or set down passengers.
Private motor cars not used for hire or reward — i.e., personal-use vehicles that do not charge passengers any fare or reward.
Goods carriages constructed or adapted for the carriage of goods rather than passengers.
Motor cycles or two-wheeled vehicles, even if used for hire, as they do not fall within the construction criteria for a motor cab.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a vehicle qualifies as a motor cab determines the type of permit required under Sections 74 and 75 of the MV Act — operators must obtain a contract carriage permit, and failure to do so attracts penal liability under the Act. It also governs applicable insurance requirements, fare regulations, fitness certificate norms, and the driver's licence category needed to legally operate the vehicle.
