definitions.definition: 'Road transport service' means a service of motor vehicles carrying passengers or goods or both by road for hire or reward, operated by a State transport undertaking under Chapter VI of this Act, and includes any such service which a State transport undertaking is authorised or required to operate under an approved scheme.
definitions.plain_english: A road transport service is an organised service run by a government-owned transport body that uses motor vehicles to carry passengers, goods, or both on public roads in exchange for payment. It is typically a state-run bus or truck service operating under a government scheme. These services are governed by special rules under the Motor Vehicles Act to ensure public interest is served.
real_world_examples: The Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation (KSRTC) operating scheduled bus routes between Bengaluru and Mysuru, collecting fares from passengers, constitutes a road transport service under the Act.
The Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation (MSRTC) running 'Shivneri' luxury bus services on inter-city routes between Mumbai and Pune for hire or reward qualifies as a road transport service.
A State transport undertaking in Rajasthan operating goods vehicles to carry agricultural produce between mandis under a notified approved scheme amounts to a road transport service.
Delhi Transport Corporation (DTC) buses running fixed routes within Delhi carrying passengers for ticket fares represent a classic road transport service operated by a state transport undertaking.

A State Government issuing a notification under Chapter VI excluding private operators from a particular route because the State transport undertaking's road transport service is being expanded to cover that corridor.
what_it_covers: Bus services operated by State Road Transport Corporations (SRTCs) carrying passengers for fares on notified routes under an approved scheme.
State transport undertaking vehicles carrying goods for hire or reward on roads under Chapter VI of the Motor Vehicles Act.
Mixed services operated by a State transport undertaking transporting both passengers and goods simultaneously on public roads for reward.
Services that a State transport undertaking is legally required or authorised to operate exclusively under a government-approved nationalisation scheme, excluding private operators from those routes.
what_it_excludes: Private bus operators or contract carriage operators running services for hire or reward, as they are not State transport undertakings.
Personal or private use of motor vehicles not operated for hire or reward, such as a government department's staff bus not charging fares.
Services operated by educational institution buses, which are used solely for transporting students and staff and not for public hire or reward.
Goods carriages operated by private individuals or companies carrying goods for hire under a private permit, as they are not part of a State transport undertaking's road transport service.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a service as a 'road transport service' under Chapter VI determines whether a State transport undertaking can seek exclusive rights over a route through an approved scheme, thereby displacing private operators and triggering the permit grant or cancellation regime under Sections 97–100 of the Act. It also governs the legal obligations, compensation entitlements, and operational conditions applicable exclusively to State transport undertakings, distinguishing them from private permit holders.

definitions.definition: "route" means a line of travel which specifies the highway which may be used between one terminus and another terminus; it includes the termini and all places on or adjacent to the line of travel which are specified as stopping places in the permit or time-table of the vehicle.
definitions.plain_english: A route is the specific road path that a public transport vehicle is officially allowed to travel between two fixed endpoints, called termini. It includes all the designated stops along that road where passengers can board or alight. Think of it as the officially approved map of roads a bus must follow, from its starting point to its final destination.
real_world_examples: A state road transport corporation bus operating between Delhi's Kashmere Gate ISBT and Dehradun Bus Stand via NH-58 is assigned a specific route covering all intermediate stops like Meerut, Muzaffarnagar, and Roorkee, and the permit specifies this exact route.

A private stage carriage operator in Kerala applies for a permit to operate on the Thiruvananthapuram to Thrissur route via NH-544, with authorised stops at Kollam, Alappuzha, and Kochi, making that entire corridor its legally defined route.

A tourist vehicle operating between Jaipur and Agra on NH-21 is issued a permit specifying the route; deviating onto an unauthorised road without permission constitutes a violation of the permit conditions under Section 192A.

A city bus service in Bengaluru running on Route No. 500C from Kempegowda Bus Station to Electronic City via Silk Board Junction has its specific road corridor and stops defined as its route in the permit, and BMTC is legally bound to operate only on that specified corridor.

An inter-state contract carriage operating between Hyderabad and Chennai is granted a permit specifying the route via NH-44, and any deviation to pick up passengers on an alternative highway without countersignature from the Tamil Nadu authority would be an unauthorised route operation.
what_it_covers: The specific highway or road alignment between two termini on which a stage carriage, contract carriage or other public service vehicle is authorised to operate under its permit.
All intermediate stopping places designated in the permit or time-table of the vehicle along the line of travel between the two termini.
Inter-state routes crossing state boundaries where both states' transport authorities must countersign or coordinate the permit, as contemplated under Sections 70 and 99.
Notified routes declared by the State Government under Section 99 where a scheme for road transport may be framed, restricting private operators.
The corridor used to determine whether an offence under Section 192A has been committed by operating a vehicle beyond the authorised route limits.
what_it_excludes: Random or casual trips taken by contract carriages engaged on a time basis without reference to any fixed road alignment between two points, since such vehicles are not necessarily bound to a specified route.
The internal movement of goods carriages on private premises or off-road agricultural tracks that are not classified as public roads or highways.
The path taken by a private motor car or private service vehicle used solely for personal or organisational purposes, as these do not require a route-specific permit.
Diversions ordered by police or traffic authorities due to emergencies or road closures, which are temporary deviations and do not constitute a change in the legally sanctioned route.
Airport tarmac roads, railway sidings, or other restricted-access infrastructure not accessible as a public road or highway.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of route is legally critical because a permit under Chapter V is granted specifically for a defined route, and operating a stage carriage or other public service vehicle outside the authorised route constitutes an offence under Section 192A, attracting cancellation of permit and monetary penalties. It also determines jurisdiction of the Regional Transport Authority under Sections 70, 72, and 80, and governs whether a State transport undertaking can establish a monopoly on a notified route under Section 99.

definitions.definition: A running board is an external step or platform affixed to the side of a motor vehicle, situated below the doors, which is not part of the enclosed body of the vehicle and is not a designated passenger space. Under the Motor Vehicles Act, no person shall ride upon or be carried on the running board of a motor vehicle, and no driver or person in charge shall permit any person to be so carried.
definitions.plain_english: A running board is the narrow step-like ledge attached to the outside of a vehicle, typically found below the doors, that people sometimes use to step in or out. The law strictly prohibits anyone from travelling on this ledge while the vehicle is moving. Both the person hanging on the running board and the driver who allows it can be penalised.
real_world_examples: A tempo traveller in rural Uttar Pradesh carries extra passengers on the side running board due to overcrowding, with the driver fully aware — both the driver and the passengers riding on the board violate Section 123 of the Motor Vehicles Act.

During a festival rush in Maharashtra, a state transport bus allows several passengers to cling to the running board due to full seating capacity, exposing the conductor and driver to prosecution under the Act.

In a Kolkata suburb, labourers hang off the running board of a pickup truck transporting workers to a construction site — the owner and driver are liable under Section 123 for permitting persons to travel outside the vehicle body.

A jeep taxi in a hill district of Himachal Pradesh carries passengers on its running board along a mountain route — a traffic police officer can immediately book the driver for this offence, which also constitutes a road safety hazard.

During an election campaign in Bihar, supporters ride on the running boards of SUVs in a rally procession — each such person and the respective drivers are in violation of Section 123 of the Motor Vehicles Act.
what_it_covers: The external step-ledge or footboard fitted on the sides of motor vehicles such as jeeps, buses, or trucks, below the door level, that is outside the enclosed passenger body.
Any platform, step, or board affixed externally to the vehicle that a person can stand or sit on while the vehicle is in motion, which is not enclosed within the vehicle's body.
Situations where persons are found clinging to or being carried on such external boards, whether with or without the driver's permission, triggering liability under Section 123.
what_it_excludes: The interior body or enclosed passenger compartment of the vehicle, where passengers are legally permitted to travel.
The bonnet or top of the vehicle, which are separately prohibited spaces under Section 123 and are not considered part of the running board.
Designated footrests or platforms that form part of the enclosed body structure of specially designed vehicles such as fire tenders or military vehicles used in official duty.
Temporary step ladders or equipment used only when the vehicle is stationary for loading or unloading purposes, not while the vehicle is in motion.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person is found on the running board determines criminal liability under Section 123 of the Motor Vehicles Act — the driver or person in charge commits an offence by permitting such carriage, and the rider commits an offence by travelling there, both attracting penalties. It also has direct implications for third-party insurance claims and accident compensation, as injuries sustained while illegally riding on a running board may affect the victim's entitlement to compensation.

definitions.definition: The Schedule, as referred to in Section 116 of the Motor Vehicles Act, means the First Schedule appended to the Act which sets forth the size, colour, type, and meanings of traffic signs, including those in Part A designating main roads, and which may be amended by the Central Government by notification in the Official Gazette to conform with any International Convention relating to motor traffic to which the Central Government is a party.
definitions.plain_english: The Schedule is a formal list attached to the Motor Vehicles Act that describes every official traffic sign used on Indian roads — including its shape, size, colour, and what it means. It acts as the authoritative reference guide for all standardised road signs in India. State governments and local authorities must follow this Schedule when putting up traffic signs, and any changes to it can only be made by the Central Government through an official notification.
real_world_examples: A municipal corporation in Pune erects a 'No Entry' sign on a one-way road; the sign must match the size, colour, and design prescribed in the First Schedule to the Motor Vehicles Act to be legally valid and enforceable.

The National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) designates NH-48 (Delhi–Mumbai corridor) as a main road by erecting the appropriate traffic sign listed in Part A of the Schedule at the relevant junctions, as required under Section 116(2).

A State Government in Tamil Nadu adds a Tamil script transcription below a speed-limit sign on state highways; this is permitted under Section 116(3) provided the transcription matches the size and colour of the original text set forth in the Schedule.

The Central Government issues a Gazette notification to amend the First Schedule to align Indian road signs with updated Vienna Convention on Road Signs and Signals standards, thereby automatically updating the legally recognised sign designs across all Indian roads.

A private builder in Gurugram erects a sign near a construction site that resembles a mandatory traffic sign from the Schedule; a Superintendent of Police can order its removal under Section 116(5) as it is misleadingly similar to an official Schedule sign.

A Regional Transport Authority in Mumbai checks whether a newly installed pedestrian crossing sign on a city route conforms to the dimensions and colour codes specified in the Schedule before certifying the road for public use.
what_it_covers: All standardised traffic signs with prescribed size, colour, type, and statutory meaning as set out in the First Schedule to the Motor Vehicles Act.
Signs listed in Part A of the Schedule used by State Governments or authorised authorities to officially designate certain roads as main roads.
The procedure and authority for amending the Schedule by Central Government notification to conform with International Conventions on motor traffic to which India is a party.
Permitted additions to Schedule signs by State Governments, such as regional language script transcriptions of the same size and colour as the original sign text.
what_it_excludes: Unofficial or private signage placed by individuals, builders, or commercial entities that do not conform to the Schedule specifications, even if they resemble traffic signs.
Signs or advertisements placed near roads that are not erected under the authority of Section 116(1), which have no legal standing as traffic signs under the Act.
Any modifications or additions to Schedule signs that differ in size or colour from the original text, as such variations are expressly prohibited under Section 116(3).
Traffic signs placed or erected prior to the commencement of the Act that do not conform to the Schedule, except where they are deemed valid under the transitional provision of Section 116(4).
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a traffic sign qualifies as a Schedule sign determines whether a driver can be legally prosecuted under Section 119 for disobeying it, since only signs placed in accordance with the Schedule carry enforceable legal authority. Non-conforming signs have no statutory backing, meaning violations cannot attract penalties, and authorities erecting non-Schedule signs may act without lawful power under the Act.

definitions.definition: Scheduled castes, as used in Section 71 of the Motor Vehicles Act, refers to those castes, races or tribes or parts of or groups within such castes, races or tribes as are deemed under Article 341 of the Constitution of India to be Scheduled Castes in relation to any State or Union Territory, for whom a percentage of stage carriage permits must be reserved by the State Government and Regional Transport Authority in the same ratio as direct recruitment appointments to public services in that State.
definitions.plain_english: Scheduled Castes are specific communities that have historically faced severe social discrimination and are officially listed by the President of India under the Constitution. In the context of the Motor Vehicles Act, the government must set aside a certain proportion of stage carriage (bus) permits specifically for people from these communities. This reservation is calculated using the same percentage as used for government job reservations in that State.
real_world_examples: In Maharashtra, where the Scheduled Caste population includes communities such as Mahars and Chambhars, the State Government fixes a percentage of stage carriage permits — say 13% mirroring direct recruitment quotas — exclusively for applicants belonging to these communities, allowing them to operate bus routes in cities like Pune with populations exceeding five lakhs.

A Dalit entrepreneur in Tamil Nadu applying for a stage carriage permit in Chennai is eligible to be considered under the reserved quota for Scheduled Castes, giving him access to a permit that might otherwise be unavailable due to competition from larger operators.

In Uttar Pradesh, when the number of stage carriage permits is fixed for Lucknow city routes, the Regional Transport Authority sets aside a proportionate number of permits for Scheduled Caste applicants as directed by the State Government, in line with the State's public service direct recruitment reservation percentage.

A co-operative society in Karnataka formed exclusively by members of Scheduled Caste communities registers to apply for reserved stage carriage permits in Bengaluru, benefiting both from the SC reservation under Section 71 and the preference given to co-operative societies under the same section.

In Andhra Pradesh, when the Central Government directs the State to limit stage carriages in Hyderabad (population over five lakhs), the State Government notifies that 15% of the capped permits are reserved for Scheduled Castes, matching the State's SC direct recruitment ratio, ensuring economic empowerment through transport entrepreneurship.
what_it_covers: Individuals belonging to castes, races, or tribes officially notified as Scheduled Castes by Presidential Order under Article 341 of the Constitution for a particular State or Union Territory, applying for stage carriage permits.

Co-operative societies or groups whose members are exclusively or predominantly from Scheduled Caste communities, seeking reserved stage carriage permits in cities with populations of five lakhs or more.

Applicants who produce a valid caste certificate issued by a competent authority of the relevant State Government confirming their Scheduled Caste status, making them eligible for the reserved permit quota under Section 71.

Persons belonging to Scheduled Castes who have converted to Buddhism (Navayana Buddhism), as they remain classified as Scheduled Castes under the relevant Presidential Orders in most States and are thus eligible for reserved permits.
what_it_excludes: Members of Scheduled Tribes, who form a separate and distinct category under Article 342 of the Constitution and have their own separate reservation of stage carriage permits alongside Scheduled Castes under Section 71.

Other Backward Classes (OBCs) and Extremely Backward Classes (EBCs), who may benefit from separate State-level schemes but are not included within the definition of Scheduled Castes for the purpose of this permit reservation.

Persons who originally belonged to a Scheduled Caste community but have converted to Islam or Christianity, as Presidential Orders generally exclude such converts from Scheduled Caste status, making them ineligible for the reserved stage carriage permits.

Individuals from economically weaker sections or below poverty line categories who do not belong to any constitutionally notified Scheduled Caste, even if they face similar socioeconomic disadvantages.

Applicants from States or Union Territories where the particular caste is not notified as a Scheduled Caste — Scheduled Caste status being State-specific under the Constitution, a person notified as SC in one State is not automatically eligible in another State.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an applicant qualifies as belonging to the Scheduled Castes directly determines their eligibility for the mandatory reserved quota of stage carriage permits that the Regional Transport Authority is legally obligated to set aside under Section 71, and failure by the authority to honour this reservation constitutes a statutory violation. This classification triggers the State Government's obligation to calculate and notify the exact percentage of reserved permits, creating an enforceable right for SC applicants to be considered separately from the general pool of stage carriage permit applications.

definitions.definition: Scheduled tribes means the tribes or tribal communities or parts of or groups within such tribes or tribal communities as are specified under Article 342 of the Constitution of India. Under the Motor Vehicles Act, scheduled tribes are a constitutionally recognised category of persons for whom a reserved percentage of stage carriage permits must be set aside by State Governments and Regional Transport Authorities, in the same ratio as direct recruitment reservations to public services in the State.
definitions.plain_english: Scheduled tribes are groups of indigenous and tribal communities officially listed by the President of India under the Constitution, recognised as historically disadvantaged. In the context of the Motor Vehicles Act, this means that when the government limits the number of stage carriage (bus) permits in large cities, a fixed share of those permits must be reserved for people belonging to these tribal communities. The proportion of permits reserved is the same as the reservation percentage used for government jobs filled by direct recruitment in that State.
real_world_examples: In Maharashtra, when the State Government caps the number of stage carriage permits for city bus routes in Mumbai (population over 5 lakh), it must reserve a percentage of those permits for applicants belonging to Scheduled Tribes such as the Warli or Gond communities, mirroring the ST reservation percentage used in State government jobs.

A Regional Transport Authority in Jharkhand, after the State Government fixes the total number of bus permits for Ranchi city routes, is legally required to set aside a specific number of those permits for ST applicants such as members of the Santhal or Munda communities before considering general applications.

An ST applicant from the Bhil community in Rajasthan applies for a stage carriage permit in Jaipur under the reserved quota; the Regional Transport Authority must process and grant that application within the reserved slots before entertaining open-category applications.

In Odisha, the State Transport Authority issues a notification fixing 200 stage carriage permits for Bhubaneswar city routes; as per Section 71, a proportion equivalent to the ST direct recruitment reservation percentage (e.g., 22.5% under central norms) must be reserved exclusively for Scheduled Tribe applicants such as the Kondh or Saura communities.

A person from the Toda tribe in Tamil Nadu who holds a valid stage carriage operator's licence applies for a city bus permit in Chennai under the ST reserved category, and the Regional Transport Authority is obligated to consider that application under the reserved quota before allotting permits to general-category applicants.
what_it_covers: Individuals belonging to tribes or tribal communities specified in the Presidential Order under Article 342 of the Constitution for the relevant State or Union Territory.

Members of tribal groups or sub-groups (parts of or groups within scheduled tribes) as notified, who apply for stage carriage permits in cities with a population of not less than five lakhs where permit numbers are capped.

Applicants from ST communities seeking reserved stage carriage permits whose reservation ratio is determined by the same percentage as ST reservations in direct recruitment to public services in the State.
Tribal cooperative societies or associations whose members collectively qualify as Scheduled Tribes and apply for reserved stage carriage permits under Section 71.
what_it_excludes: Persons belonging to Scheduled Castes, who form a separate and distinct reserved category under Section 71 and are governed by their own quota distinct from the Scheduled Tribes quota.
Other Backward Classes (OBC) or Economically Weaker Sections (EWS), who are not covered by the Scheduled Tribes definition and have no reserved quota under Section 71 of the Motor Vehicles Act.

General category applicants or those belonging to communities not notified under Article 342 of the Constitution as Scheduled Tribes for the relevant State, even if they are socially or economically disadvantaged.

State transport undertakings, co-operative societies not composed of ST members, and ex-servicemen who receive preference under a separate proviso in Section 71 rather than through the ST reserved quota mechanism.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an applicant qualifies as a member of a Scheduled Tribe directly determines their eligibility for the reserved percentage of stage carriage permits mandated under Section 71, giving them a right to be considered within the protected quota before open-category applications are processed. definitions.definition: A 'scheme' under the Motor Vehicles Act means either: (a) a scheme made by the Central Government by notification in the Official Gazette under Section 75 for regulating the business of renting of motor cabs or motor cycles; or (b) a scheme formulated and published by a State Government under Sections 99–100 for providing road transport service through a State transport undertaking in relation to any area or route, which upon final approval becomes the 'approved scheme'.
definitions.plain_english: A 'scheme' is an official government plan published in the Official Gazette that sets out rules for a specific transport-related purpose. It can be a Central Government plan regulating how motor cabs or motorcycles are rented out to the public, or a State Government plan to run bus or road transport services in a particular area, sometimes to the exclusion of private operators. Once a State scheme goes through a process of public objection and approval, it becomes legally binding as the 'approved scheme'.
real_world_examples: The Central Government notifies a scheme under Section 75 allowing licensed operators in Mumbai to rent self-drive motorcycles to customers, specifying licensing conditions, record-keeping requirements, and rental terms.

The Karnataka State Government formulates a scheme under Section 99 proposing that KSRTC exclusively operate bus services on the Bengaluru–Mysuru route, publishes it in the Karnataka Gazette, and after hearing objections, approves it — making it an 'approved scheme' binding on private operators.

The Delhi Government publishes a proposal for a scheme to have Delhi Transport Corporation run services on certain inter-district routes, receives objections from private permit holders, and modifies the scheme before final publication in the Official Gazette.

definitions.definition: A semi-trailer is a trailer which is so constructed that a part thereof rests upon and is supported by, or is designed to rest upon and be supported by, a motor vehicle, transmitting a part of its weight to the drawing vehicle.
definitions.plain_english: A semi-trailer is a type of trailer that does not have a front axle and instead relies on the rear portion of a truck or tractor for support, with the front end resting on and being carried by the towing vehicle. Unlike a full trailer which has its own front wheels, a semi-trailer transfers part of its weight to the vehicle pulling it. Together, the towing vehicle and semi-trailer form what is commonly called an articulated vehicle or 'truck-trailer' combination seen on Indian highways.
real_world_examples: A Tata or Ashok Leyland truck-tractor unit coupled to a long flatbed cargo-carrying trailer at Nhava Sheva (JNPT) port in Mumbai, used to transport shipping containers to inland container depots — the trailer's front rests on the tractor's fifth wheel, making it a classic semi-trailer.

A petroleum tanker trailer attached to a prime mover on the Delhi–Mumbai National Highway, where the tanker unit has rear axles but no front axle of its own and depends on the tractor unit for front support and steering.

A refrigerated (reefer) semi-trailer hauling perishable goods like vegetables from Nashik farms to markets in Bengaluru, attached to a heavy goods tractor unit registered under the MV Act and requiring a valid permit under Section 66.

A low-bed semi-trailer used to transport heavy construction machinery such as a JCB excavator or road-roller from a Pune equipment depot to a highway construction site in Rajasthan, requiring special permits given the oversize load.

A car-carrier semi-trailer transporting newly manufactured Maruti Suzuki vehicles from the Manesar plant in Haryana to dealerships across northern India, operating under a goods carriage permit as an articulated vehicle combination.
what_it_covers: A flatbed trailer with rear axles only, whose front end rests on and is coupled to a truck tractor via a fifth-wheel coupling, used for carrying containerised or bulk cargo on Indian roads.
A tanker trailer (for petroleum, chemicals, or liquid goods) that has no front axle and is structurally dependent on the prime mover for front support and directional control.
A low-bed or drop-deck trailer designed to carry over-dimensional cargo such as industrial equipment or transformers, where the front of the trailer rests on the towing tractor unit.
A refrigerated (reefer) trailer without a front axle, attached to a heavy tractor unit for transporting perishable goods across state borders in India.
what_it_excludes: A full trailer, which has both front and rear axles of its own and does not rest upon or transfer weight to the drawing motor vehicle, and thus is not a semi-trailer.
A motor vehicle that is itself self-propelled — the semi-trailer has no engine or propulsion mechanism of its own and cannot move independently on a road.
A simple drawbar trailer (dog trailer) that is entirely supported on its own wheels and merely towed by a vehicle without any weight being transmitted to the towing unit.
A caravan or camping trailer that is fully supported on its own axles and only connected to a motor car by a tow hitch without bearing any weight on the towing vehicle.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a vehicle qualifies as a semi-trailer determines whether the combined unit must be classified and registered as an 'articulated vehicle' under Section 2, triggering specific permit requirements under Section 66 for operating as a goods carriage, as well as applicable gross vehicle weight limits, fitness certificate standards, and driver licensing category requirements for the tractor-trailer combination.

definitions.definition: The Solatium Fund refers to the fund established under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 (4 of 1939), as it stood immediately before the commencement of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, for the purpose of providing compensation to victims of hit and run motor accidents, and which continues to be administered under schemes framed by the Central Government under Section 163 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988.
definitions.plain_english: The Solatium Fund is a special government-backed fund created to pay compensation to people who are killed or seriously injured in road accidents where the vehicle responsible either flees the scene or cannot be identified. It acts as a safety net so that victims or their families are not left without any financial relief simply because the guilty driver cannot be traced. The fund is managed by the General Insurance Corporation of India under a scheme notified by the Central Government.
real_world_examples: A pedestrian in Bengaluru is knocked down and killed by an unidentified speeding truck that flees without stopping; the victim's family applies for compensation under the Solatium Fund scheme since the vehicle owner cannot be traced.

A motorcyclist in rural Rajasthan is severely injured by a hit and run car at night on a state highway; as the car's registration cannot be determined, the injured person claims from the Solatium Fund for grievous hurt compensation.

A daily-wage worker in Mumbai is fatally struck by an unknown vehicle while crossing the road; his widow files a claim with the designated authority under the Solatium Fund scheme administered by the General Insurance Corporation.

A cyclist in Chennai sustains permanent disability after being hit by a vehicle that drove away; since no insurer or owner can be identified, the claim is routed through the Solatium Fund to provide statutory minimum compensation.

A family in Uttar Pradesh whose breadwinner died in a hit and run accident on a National Highway in 2001 seeks retrospective benefit under the Solatium Fund scheme, which may operate from the date of establishment of the fund under the 1939 Act, provided no prejudice is caused to any affected party.
what_it_covers: Compensation paid to legal representatives of persons killed in hit and run motor accidents where the offending vehicle cannot be identified.
Compensation for victims who suffer grievous hurt in a hit and run accident and cannot pursue a normal insurance claim due to the unknown identity of the vehicle or its owner.

Claims administered by the General Insurance Corporation under a scheme framed by the Central Government, including retrospective claims dating back to the establishment of the fund under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939.
Cases where the offending vehicle is identified but the owner/insurer is untraceable, making the Solatium Fund the only available avenue for statutory relief.
what_it_excludes: Accidents where the offending vehicle and its owner or insurer are clearly identified, as such claims are handled through the normal motor accident claims process before a Claims Tribunal.
Compensation claims arising from accidents that are not classified as 'hit and run motor accidents' under the Act, such as accidents involving known parties with valid insurance.
Retrospective claims that would prejudicially affect the interests of any person already governed by a provision of the scheme, as explicitly protected by the proviso in Section 163.
Compensation for minor injuries or property damage — the Solatium Fund scheme under MV Act primarily addresses death and grievous hurt, not trivial bodily harm or vehicle damage.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a case qualifies for relief under the Solatium Fund determines whether a victim or their family can receive any statutory compensation at all when the responsible vehicle or driver cannot be identified; without this fund, such victims would be entirely without legal remedy. It triggers the obligation of the General Insurance Corporation and designated scheme authorities to process and disburse compensation, and non-compliance with the scheme's provisions can attract criminal penalties including imprisonment and fines under Section 163.

definitions.definition: A special permit issued under sub-section (8) of section 88 of the Motor Vehicles Act, authorising a motor vehicle to operate under conditions or for purposes that are distinct from those covered by a regular, temporary, or countersigned permit, and which is not subject to the standard five-year duration prescribed under section 81 for ordinary permits.
definitions.plain_english: A special permit is a specific type of authorisation granted under the Motor Vehicles Act that allows a vehicle to be used for a particular journey or purpose that falls outside the scope of a normal permit. Unlike a regular permit which lasts five years, a special permit is typically of shorter or defined duration and is issued for exceptional or one-off circumstances. It allows transport authorities to grant permission for vehicles to operate in situations not covered by standard permit categories.
real_world_examples: A private bus operator in Maharashtra obtains a special permit under Section 88(8) to transport a wedding party from Mumbai to Goa for a single trip, as no regular contract carriage permit covers that specific cross-state journey.

A school in Delhi hires an additional bus during annual examination season and the operator obtains a special permit to operate a vehicle temporarily for that defined purpose without holding a full-term educational institution bus permit.

A tour operator in Rajasthan secures a special permit to move a fleet of vehicles for a government-organised cultural festival procession for a fixed short-duration period that does not justify a five-year permit.

A transport company in Tamil Nadu is granted a special permit to ferry factory workers during a specific industrial strike period when regular stage carriage services are disrupted, covering a defined short-term operational need.

A vehicle owner in Uttar Pradesh receives a special permit to carry goods for a relief operation during a flood emergency, authorising inter-regional operation without going through the full countersignature process required for regular permits.
what_it_covers: Vehicles authorised to operate for a specific, defined purpose or journey not covered by a regular permit, issued under Section 88(8) of the MV Act.
Motor vehicles operating under conditions that do not conform to the standard five-year permit validity and are explicitly carved out from the duration provisions of Section 81.
Cross-regional or cross-state vehicle operations granted on a case-specific basis by the appropriate transport authority for a limited and defined period or occasion.
Vehicles used for emergency, ceremonial, relief, or one-time commercial purposes where a full regular permit is neither practical nor warranted.
what_it_excludes: Regular permits granted under the standard permit framework, which are subject to the five-year duration and renewal provisions under Section 81.
Temporary permits issued under Section 87, which are a separate and distinct category governed by different provisions of the Act.
Countersigned permits under Section 88(1), which are extensions of primary permits and follow their own validity synchronisation rules rather than operating as special permits.
National permits issued for goods carriages that already carry cross-state validity under a separate prescribed framework.
Stage carriage permits, contract carriage permits, or goods carriage permits issued through the standard application and grant process under Chapter V of the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a permit qualifies as a special permit under Section 88(8) directly determines whether the standard five-year duration and renewal obligations under Section 81 apply, exempting the holder from those timelines and associated compliance requirements. Operating a vehicle beyond the scope or duration of a special permit, or without obtaining one where required, constitutes an offence under the Act and can lead to prosecution, permit cancellation, and vehicle detention.

definitions.definition: Speed limits refer to the maximum speed or minimum speed fixed for a motor vehicle under the Motor Vehicles Act or by or under any other law for the time being in force, as applicable to motor vehicles driven in any public place, including such limits as may be fixed by the Central Government by notification in the Official Gazette or by the State Government or any authority authorised by it in the interest of public safety, convenience, or because of the nature of any road or bridge, communicated through appropriate traffic signs erected under section 116.
definitions.plain_english: Speed limits are the legally fixed upper (maximum) and lower (minimum) speeds at which a vehicle can be driven on public roads in India. The central government sets the absolute maximum speeds, while state governments can set lower or specific limits for particular roads, areas, or types of vehicles. These limits are displayed through road signs so that drivers are informed of the permitted speed range.
real_world_examples: On a National Highway in Maharashtra, the Central Government fixes a maximum speed of 120 km/h for cars; a driver caught doing 150 km/h is in violation of the speed limits under Section 112 and is liable to penalty under Section 183.

The Delhi Traffic Police, authorised by the State Government, erects signs on a congested stretch of Chandni Chowk restricting motor vehicles to 20 km/h due to heavy pedestrian traffic — any vehicle exceeding this speed violates the applicable speed limit.

A school zone in Bengaluru is notified by the Karnataka State Government with a maximum speed limit of 25 km/h for all motor vehicles during school hours; a tempo driver doing 50 km/h through this zone is penalised under Section 183.

A truck driver on a hilly stretch of NH-44 in Himachal Pradesh where a minimum speed limit of 30 km/h has been fixed drives at 15 km/h, blocking traffic and violating the minimum speed limit provisions under Section 112.

A person convicted for overspeeding has the endorsement noted on his driving licence; if no further offence occurs for one year, he becomes entitled under Section 25 to receive a new driving licence free from the speed-limit-related endorsement.

The Central Government issues a gazette notification capping the maximum speed for heavy goods vehicles on expressways at 80 km/h; a lorry owner or operator allowing the driver to exceed this limit is jointly liable under Section 183.
what_it_covers: Maximum speed limits fixed by the Central Government by gazette notification applicable to all motor vehicles or specific classes on public roads.
Minimum speed limits fixed by the State Government or authorised authority for particular roads, bridges, or areas in the interest of public safety or convenience.
Speed restrictions of limited duration (up to one month) imposed without a formal gazette notification by the State Government or authorised authority.
Speed limits specific to motor vehicles to which a trailer is attached, as notified by the State Government.
Speed limit signs erected under Section 116 that give legal notice of applicable speed limits to road users.
what_it_excludes: Vehicles registered under Section 60 being used during military manoeuvres within areas and periods specified under the Manoeuvres, Field Firing and Artillery Practice Act, 1938, which are exempt from Section 112.
Speed standards or performance benchmarks set by the manufacturer for vehicles that are not legally notified as enforceable speed limits under this Act or any other law.
Internal private roads or premises not constituting a 'public place' as defined under the Act, where public speed limit provisions do not apply.
Speed restrictions imposed solely under municipal or local body bye-laws that have not been authorised or notified as speed limits under this Act.
Speed-related guidelines or advisories issued by road authorities that are not backed by a gazette notification or an authorised traffic sign as required by Section 112.
definitions.why_it_matters: Violation of speed limits constitutes an offence under Section 183 of the Motor Vehicles Act, attracting fines and potential imprisonment, and triggers a mandatory endorsement on the offending driver's driving licence under Section 25. The classification of an offence as a speed limit violation also determines the reduced one-year (instead of three-year) waiting period for obtaining a fresh endorsement-free driving licence.

definitions.plain_english: A stage carriage is a bus or large vehicle that picks up and drops off members of the public at different stops along a route, charging each passenger a separate fare for their portion of the journey. Think of a regular city bus or an inter-city bus where different passengers board and alight at different points, each paying their own ticket price. It is the most common form of public road transport in India used by ordinary commuters.
real_world_examples: A KSRTC (Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation) bus operating on the Bengaluru to Mysuru route, stopping at multiple intermediate points like Channapatna and Mandya, collecting individual fares from each passenger — this is a classic stage carriage.

A private mini-bus plying the Delhi–Gurgaon stretch, picking up office commuters at different bus stops along NH-48 and charging each passenger a separate fare for their respective distance — qualifies as a stage carriage.

A DTC (Delhi Transport Corporation) city bus operating on route 423 within Delhi, stopping at designated bus stops and issuing separate tickets to each boarding passenger — a typical urban stage carriage operation.

A privately owned Tata bus operating as a rural transport service between two tehsil towns in Rajasthan, collecting individual fares from villagers boarding at different village stops along the route — regulated as a stage carriage under the Motor Vehicles Act.

A local 'share jeep' or 'share auto' operating in hilly areas of Himachal Pradesh or Uttarakhand, carrying passengers between hill stations with separate fares charged per seat per distance covered — may be classified as a stage carriage depending on passenger capacity.

Private operators running mini-buses or full-sized buses on stage carriage permits, picking up and dropping passengers at intermediate stops along a notified route.
City or town buses operated by local municipal transport undertakings charging separate fares to each boarding passenger.
Ordinary class inter-district buses plying between two towns and stopping at intermediate villages to pick up passengers on a per-seat fare basis.
Rural feeder buses operating on approved routes connecting villages to district headquarters with individual ticketing for each passenger.
what_it_excludes: Contract carriages (e.g., chartered buses, tourist coaches) where the entire vehicle is hired under a single contract and no separate fares are charged to individual passengers.
Maxicabs and motorcabs (taxis) carrying passengers for hire or reward as a single unit without charging stage-wise separate fares.
Private service vehicles used for transporting employees of a company or institution without charging individual fares.
Educational institution buses owned by schools or colleges used solely for transporting students and staff, not the general public.
Goods carriages that carry goods and not passengers for individual fares, even if incidentally persons are present.

definitions.definition: A stage carriage permit is a permit granted or countersigned by a Regional or State Transport Authority authorising the use of a motor vehicle as a stage carriage on a specified route or area, and which, subject to any conditions specified therein, also authorises the use of the vehicle as a contract carriage and may authorise its use as a goods carriage either when carrying passengers or not.
definitions.plain_english: A stage carriage permit is an official licence that allows a bus or similar vehicle to pick up and drop off passengers at fixed stops along a set route, charging separate fares. Think of it as the government's permission slip for running a public bus service. The same permit can also allow the vehicle to be used as a private hire coach or even to carry goods under certain conditions.
real_world_examples: A private bus operator in Tamil Nadu obtains a stage carriage permit from the Regional Transport Authority, Chennai, to run a daily bus service between Chennai and Coimbatore, picking up passengers at designated bus stops along National Highway 544.

A Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation bus operating on the Bengaluru–Mysuru route holds a stage carriage permit, allowing it to charge separate fares to individual passengers boarding at different stops along the route.

A bus operator in Maharashtra holding a stage carriage permit uses the same vehicle during off-peak hours to carry a wedding party as a contract carriage under the conditions specified in the permit, without obtaining a separate contract carriage permit.

A Rajasthan-based transport company running a rural feeder bus service between Jaipur and nearby villages operates under a stage carriage permit issued by the Rajasthan State Transport Authority, ensuring compliance with prescribed routes, timetables, and seating capacity conditions.

A school bus operator in Hyderabad applies for a stage carriage permit to run a scheduled service picking up students from multiple residential colonies, with the permit specifying maximum speed limits, number of daily trips, and vehicle maintenance requirements.
what_it_covers: A permit authorising a bus or omnibus to ply on a specified route picking up and dropping passengers at fixed stops for separate fares.
Conditional authorisation to use the same stage carriage vehicle as a contract carriage, subject to conditions specified in the permit.
Conditional authorisation to use the stage carriage vehicle as a goods carriage, whether or not passengers are being carried, subject to permit conditions.
Reserve stage carriage vehicles intended to maintain the service and provide for special occasions on the approved route.
Operation of a stage carriage on an inter-State route where the permit has been countersigned by the relevant Regional or State Transport Authority of the other State.
what_it_excludes: A contract carriage permit, which authorises a vehicle solely for hire as a whole unit without picking up passengers at intermediate stops for separate fares.
A goods carriage permit, which authorises the carriage of goods only and does not by itself allow the carriage of fare-paying passengers at separate fares.
Private service vehicles, invalid carriages, and educational institution buses that do not charge separate fares to individual members of the public.
Transport vehicles owned by the Central or State Government used for non-commercial government purposes, which are exempt from the permit requirement entirely.
Vehicles with a gross vehicle weight not exceeding 3,000 kilograms used as goods vehicles, which are exempt from the permit requirement under Section 66.
definitions.why_it_matters: Operating a stage carriage without a valid stage carriage permit is an offence under the Motor Vehicles Act, exposing the owner to penalties, seizure of the vehicle, and cancellation of registration; the nature of the permit also determines whether the vehicle may legally carry contract passengers or goods, and failure to hold the correct permit class can invalidate insurance coverage and expose the operator to unlimited third-party liability.

definitions.definition: State Government, in the context of the Motor Vehicles Act, refers to the Government of a State in India, and in relation to a Union Territory, means the Administrator thereof appointed under Article 239 of the Constitution; it is the authority empowered to issue notifications, frame rules, specify areas, and exercise regulatory powers conferred upon it under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: The 'State Government' means the elected government of a particular Indian State, responsible for making and enforcing road transport rules within that State. For Union Territories, it refers to the Administrator (Lieutenant Governor or equivalent) who acts in place of a State Government. It is the primary authority that can issue notifications, set policies, and regulate motor vehicle matters at the State level.
real_world_examples: The Government of Maharashtra issuing a notification under Section 26 specifying the minimum qualifications and standards for licensing authorities within the State.
The Government of Tamil Nadu exercising powers under Section 136 to prescribe the manner in which police officers may inspect vehicles and demand production of documents on public roads.
The Delhi Administration (as the State Government for the Union Territory of Delhi) notifying specific areas for the purpose of regulating stage carriage permits and route operations.
The Government of Karnataka directing its transport department to implement new registration norms for electric vehicles by issuing a gazette notification under the Act.
The Government of Uttar Pradesh specifying through a State-level notification the designated testing stations for certificate of fitness under its territorial jurisdiction.
The Puducherry Administration acting as State Government and framing rules for conductor licensing applicable within the Union Territory.
what_it_covers: The elected government of any Indian State (e.g., Government of Rajasthan, Government of West Bengal) exercising powers under the Act.
The Administrator of a Union Territory (such as the Lieutenant Governor of Jammu & Kashmir or Chandigarh) acting in the capacity of State Government.
Any department or officer of the State Government to whom the State Government has delegated its powers under the Act.
State Government's power under Section 26 to specify conditions, qualifications, and procedures for licensing authorities.
State Government's authority under Section 136 to prescribe rules for inspection of vehicles and documents by police officers.
what_it_excludes: The Central Government of India, which is a separate and distinct authority with its own powers under the Act (e.g., framing central motor vehicle rules).
Local bodies such as Municipal Corporations or Panchayats, which are not considered State Governments even though they may exercise delegated transport-related functions.
Private or quasi-governmental entities such as State Transport Undertakings, which operate under the State Government but do not constitute the State Government itself.
Courts or tribunals such as the State Transport Appellate Tribunal, which are judicial or quasi-judicial bodies distinct from the executive State Government.
Regional Transport Authorities or State Transport Authorities, which are statutory bodies created by the State but are not themselves the State Government.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of an authority as the 'State Government' determines which entity has the legal power to issue binding notifications, frame rules, and specify areas or conditions under the Act — without a valid State Government notification, regulatory actions such as area specifications under Section 26 or vehicle inspection rules under Section 136 would lack legal validity. Offences, obligations, and procedural requirements triggered by State notifications become enforceable only when issued by the correctly identified State Government authority.

definitions.definition: The State Transport Appellate Tribunal is a quasi-judicial body constituted by the State Government under sub-section (2) of Section 89 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, consisting of a judicial officer not below the rank of a District Judge or qualified to be a Judge of the High Court, exercising jurisdiction within such area as may be notified by the State Government. It hears appeals against orders of the State Transport Authority or Regional Transport Authority relating to grant, refusal, revocation, suspension, or variation of permits, and also exercises revisional jurisdiction under Section 90 over orders against which no appeal lies.
definitions.plain_english: The State Transport Appellate Tribunal is a special government-appointed court-like body set up in each state to hear complaints from people who are unhappy with decisions made by transport authorities about vehicle permits. It is headed by a senior judicial officer, at least of the level of a District Judge. Its decisions on appeals are final, and it can also review decisions of transport authorities even when no formal appeal is available.
real_world_examples: A bus operator in Maharashtra whose application for a new stage carriage permit was rejected by the Regional Transport Authority files an appeal before the State Transport Appellate Tribunal in Mumbai, which reviews the refusal and directs the RTA to grant the permit.

A truck fleet owner in Tamil Nadu whose goods carriage permit was suspended by the State Transport Authority approaches the State Transport Appellate Tribunal seeking stay of the suspension order, arguing the suspension was imposed without adequate opportunity of hearing.

A travel agency in Rajasthan aggrieved by an additional condition attached to its contract carriage permit — limiting the number of passengers — appeals before the State Transport Appellate Tribunal, which modifies the condition after hearing both parties.

An auto-rickshaw permit holder in Delhi whose application for transfer of permit under Section 82 was refused by the licensing authority invokes the appellate jurisdiction of the State Transport Appellate Tribunal to challenge the refusal.

A state transport undertaking in Karnataka that made an order against a private operator without following due process is subjected to revision proceedings before the State Transport Appellate Tribunal, which sets aside the order under Section 90 after finding it illegal.
what_it_covers: Appeals against refusal by a State or Regional Transport Authority to grant, renew, or countersign a permit under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988.
Appeals against revocation, suspension, or variation of conditions of any permit held by an aggrieved person.
Revision petitions filed under Section 90 against orders of State or Regional Transport Authorities that are illegal or improper and against which no direct appeal lies.
Appeals against refusal to transfer a permit under Section 82 or refusal to grant permission under Section 83.
Pending appeals that were initiated under the earlier Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, and were continuing at the commencement of the 1988 Act.
what_it_excludes: Appeals against directions issued by the Inter-State Transport Commission — aggrieved persons may only appeal against the consequent order of the transport authority, not the direction itself.
Matters falling within the jurisdiction of the Claims Tribunal, which deals with compensation for motor accident victims and is a separate adjudicatory body.
Criminal proceedings or prosecutions for offences under the Motor Vehicles Act, which are handled by ordinary criminal courts and not by the Tribunal.
Disputes relating to registration, fitness certificates, or driving licences, which are governed by different authorities and appeal mechanisms under the Act.
Revision applications filed after thirty days of the impugned order, unless the Tribunal is satisfied that good and sufficient cause existed for the delay.
definitions.why_it_matters: The existence and jurisdiction of the State Transport Appellate Tribunal determines whether an aggrieved permit holder has a legal remedy against arbitrary or unlawful decisions of transport authorities; its final orders under Section 89 and revisional orders under Section 90 are binding and cannot ordinarily be re-agitated before the same authority, making it the primary forum for ensuring accountability in the grant and regulation of transport permits in each state.

definitions.definition: The State Transport Authority means the authority constituted under section 68 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 for the State as a whole, empowered to grant, countersign, suspend, revoke or cancel permits for transport vehicles operating on routes or areas that extend beyond the jurisdiction of a single Regional Transport Authority, and to exercise such other powers as are conferred upon it by or under this Act.
definitions.plain_english: The State Transport Authority is the top-level government body in each State that oversees and regulates road transport across the entire State. It grants permission (called permits) for buses, trucks, and other commercial vehicles to operate on longer routes that cross multiple regions within a State. It also coordinates with Regional Transport Authorities and ensures that road transport across the State is properly controlled and regulated.
real_world_examples: When a private bus operator in Maharashtra wants to run a stage carriage service between Mumbai and Nagpur — a route crossing multiple RTA regions — they must apply to the Maharashtra State Transport Authority for a permit.

The State Transport Authority of Rajasthan receives returns from the Inspector General of Police regarding stolen vehicles such as trucks and buses, and maintains records accordingly under Section 62.

A goods carriage operator seeking a national permit to carry freight across multiple States first obtains countersignature or authorisation from the State Transport Authority of the State where the vehicle is registered.

When the State Government of Tamil Nadu issues directions under Section 67 regarding fixing of bus fares on inter-district routes, those directions are issued to the State Transport Authority, which then implements and communicates them to Regional Transport Authorities.

A contract carriage operator in Karnataka applies to the State Transport Authority for a special permit to run tourist vehicles on routes that span the entire State of Karnataka, rather than a single RTA region.

Under Section 88, the State Transport Authority countersigns a permit issued by another State's authority, enabling a Delhi-based bus operator to operate services into Haryana without requiring a fresh permit from the Haryana RTA.
what_it_covers: Granting, refusing, suspending, or revoking permits for transport vehicles operating on routes or areas extending beyond a single Regional Transport Authority's jurisdiction.
Receiving returns from the Inspector General of Police regarding stolen and recovered motor vehicles within the State.
Issuing countersignatures on permits granted by Regional Transport Authorities of other States to enable inter-state operations within the State.
Implementing directions issued by the State Government regarding fixation of fares, freights, and restrictions on goods traffic.
Granting special permits and temporary permits for transport vehicles operating across multiple regions within the State.
Exercising appellate or supervisory functions over Regional Transport Authorities in matters of permits and transport regulation.
what_it_excludes: Regional Transport Authorities, which are distinct bodies constituted for specific regions within a State and operate below the State Transport Authority in the regulatory hierarchy.

Transport vehicles owned and used exclusively by the Central Government or State Government for purposes unconnected with any commercial enterprise, which are exempt from the permit requirement under Section 66(3)(a).
The State Transport Appellate Tribunal, which is a separate quasi-judicial body empowered to hear appeals against orders of the State Transport Authority and Regional Transport Authorities.
Private individuals or operators who merely hold permits — the State Transport Authority is the regulatory body, not a permit holder or vehicle operator.

Vehicles with gross vehicle weight not exceeding 3,000 kilograms (goods vehicles), which are generally exempt from permit requirements under Section 66(3)(h) and therefore largely outside the permitting jurisdiction of the State Transport Authority.
The Central Government's prescribed authority for national permits, which operates at the national level and is distinct from the State Transport Authority.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an authority qualifies as the State Transport Authority determines the legal validity of permits, countersignatures, and regulatory directions — a permit granted or countersigned by any other body without this status would be void, exposing the vehicle owner to prosecution under Section 66 for operating a transport vehicle without a valid permit. The State Transport Authority's decisions on permit grants, refusals, suspensions, and revocations directly trigger or block the rights and liabilities of transport operators across the entire State.

definitions.definition: A summons, in the context of the Motor Vehicles Act, is a formal legal document issued by a Court directing an accused person to appear before it to answer a charge for an offence under the Act; it may also state the option for the accused to plead guilty and remit the prescribed fine without personal appearance, and when served within twenty-eight days of the commission of an offence under section 183 or 184, it satisfies a mandatory precondition for conviction.
definitions.plain_english: A summons is an official court notice sent to a person telling them they are being prosecuted for a traffic offence and must appear before the court on a specified date. In many traffic cases under this law, the notice may also give the person an option to pay a fine in advance without going to court. If the summons is not served within twenty-eight days of the offence (for certain speeding or dangerous driving cases), the accused generally cannot be convicted.
real_world_examples: A driver in Mumbai is caught speeding on the Western Express Highway by a traffic camera; the Magistrate's Court issues a summons within twenty-eight days directing the driver to appear on a specified date or pay a fine by money order to avoid further proceedings.

A motorcyclist in Delhi is charged under section 184 for dangerous driving; since the police could not warn him at the scene, a summons is sent by the court within twenty-eight days to his registered address to satisfy the precondition for conviction.

A truck owner in Chennai whose vehicle was involved in a hit-and-run receives a summons from the court under section 208, which states that he may appear through a pleader or plead guilty and remit the specified sum by money order before the hearing date.

A taxi driver in Kolkata charged with driving under the influence under section 185 has his driving licence seized by police under section 206 because the officer believes he may abscond to avoid service of the summons issued by the court.

A bus operator in Hyderabad charged with overloading under section 194 receives a court summons specifying that he may plead guilty by a prior date and forward his driving licence along with the plea, after which an endorsement of conviction is made on the licence.

A private car owner in Bengaluru finds that the prosecution against him for a speeding offence is dropped because the summons was served on the thirty-fifth day after the alleged offence, beyond the twenty-eight day window mandated by section 209.

A summons served within twenty-eight days of the commission of an offence under section 183 (speeding) or section 184 (dangerous driving), which fulfils the mandatory precondition allowing the court to proceed to conviction.
A summons issued under section 208 that specifies on its face the option to plead guilty and remit the fine by money order, or to appear in person or through a pleader.
A summons issued under section 208 that requires the accused, in cases involving licence endorsement, to forward their driving licence along with a letter containing the guilty plea.
A situation under section 206 where police may seize a driving licence because the driver may abscond to avoid service of the summons, forwarding the licence to the court taking cognizance.
what_it_excludes: A verbal warning or oral caution issued by a traffic police officer at the scene of the offence, which is a separate precondition under section 209(a) and is not a summons.
A notice sent by registered post to the accused or registered owner within fourteen days under section 209(b), which is a distinct alternative precondition and is not a summons.
An administrative challan or compounding receipt issued by a police officer under section 200 (compounding of offences), which is not a court-issued summons.
An arrest warrant issued by a court when the accused fails to appear in response to a summons, which is a separate and more coercive judicial instrument.
A notice issued by the licensing or transport authority for permit or licence-related proceedings, which is an administrative notice and not a criminal court summons under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Timely service of a summons within twenty-eight days of the offence is a mandatory legal precondition under section 209 for convicting a person of offences under sections 183 and 184; failure to serve it in time (unless excused by the proviso) is an absolute bar to conviction. Additionally, the summons triggers summary disposal procedures under section 208, determining whether the accused must appear in court or may pay a fine by money order, and whether an endorsement is made on the driving licence.

definitions.definition: A taximeter is a mechanical or electronic device fitted to a motor cab that automatically calculates and displays the fare payable by a passenger based on the distance travelled and/or time elapsed during the hiring, as prescribed under the Act. Under Section 74(2)(h), a taximeter shall be fitted and maintained in proper working order in motor cabs where so prescribed as a condition of the contract carriage permit.
definitions.plain_english: A taximeter is the meter installed inside a taxi or auto-rickshaw that automatically calculates the fare for a trip based on how far you travel and sometimes how long you wait. It ticks up as the vehicle moves, showing the passenger the exact amount to be paid at the end of the journey. Think of it as the official fare calculator attached to the vehicle.
real_world_examples: A Kaali-Peeli taxi in Mumbai is required under its contract carriage permit to have a functioning taximeter fitted on the dashboard; if the driver refuses to start the meter, the passenger can report the violation to the Regional Transport Authority.

An auto-rickshaw operator in Delhi is inspected by a traffic enforcement officer who finds the taximeter has been tampered with to run faster than the prescribed rate, resulting in cancellation of the permit condition compliance and prosecution of the driver.

A radio cab company in Bengaluru integrates a GPS-based electronic taximeter into its app-enabled vehicles so that the fare displayed digitally complies with the State Government-prescribed rates as required under the contract carriage permit conditions.

A Regional Transport Authority in Chennai conducts a surprise check and finds that several motor cabs are operating without a certified and sealed taximeter, leading to show-cause notices and suspension of their contract carriage permits under Section 74.

A passenger in Kolkata disputes the fare charged by a taxi driver; the Regional Transport Authority uses the taximeter reading log as evidence to determine whether the prescribed fare was correctly applied during the journey.

Auto-rickshaw meters that are calibrated and sealed by the prescribed authority and mandated as a condition of the contract carriage permit.
Any device affixed to or integrated into a motor cab that registers and displays the chargeable fare to the passenger in real time during the hiring.
what_it_excludes: Fare calculation systems used in stage carriages or omnibuses, which charge fixed route-based fares and are not governed by taximeter provisions.
Rate charts or printed fare tables exhibited inside motor cabs that show fixed tariffs without automated distance or time computation.
Meters or tracking devices fitted in goods carriages or private service vehicles, which are not contract carriages carrying passengers for hire.
Manual or verbal fare quotations given by drivers of vehicles other than motor cabs, which are not automated metered devices.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a taximeter is fitted and maintained in proper working order is a mandatory condition attachable to a contract carriage permit for motor cabs under Section 74(2)(h); failure to comply can result in permit conditions being varied, suspended, or cancelled by the Regional Transport Authority, and the operator may face prosecution for breach of permit conditions. The taximeter requirement directly protects passengers from overcharging and ensures fare transparency mandated under the Act.

definitions.definition: A temporary permit is a permit issued under section 87 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, which authorises the use of a transport vehicle for a limited, short-term period and is distinct from a regular permit in that it is not subject to the standard five-year duration and renewal provisions applicable to ordinary permits under section 81.
definitions.plain_english: A temporary permit is a short-duration permission given to a vehicle owner to operate a transport vehicle (like a bus or goods truck) for a limited time, without going through the full, lengthy permit process. Unlike a regular permit that lasts five years and can be renewed, a temporary permit is issued quickly for a specific, time-bound purpose such as a festival, emergency, or special event. It cannot be renewed in the same way as a regular permit and expires automatically after its short validity period.
real_world_examples: A private bus operator in Rajasthan applies for a temporary permit to run extra buses during the Pushkar Mela fair season for a few weeks when regular bus services are insufficient to meet passenger demand.

A transporter in Maharashtra obtains a temporary permit to carry agricultural produce from a rural district to a city market during the peak harvest season when regular goods carriage permits are not readily available.
A travel agency in Delhi secures a temporary permit for a fleet of tourist coaches to ferry pilgrims from various states to Vaishno Devi during the Navratri festival period.

A state-run bus service in Tamil Nadu is granted a temporary permit to operate additional services between Chennai and Tirupati during a special religious occasion, supplementing the existing regular permit holders.

A school in Pune obtains a temporary permit for a hired bus to transport students for an outstation educational excursion spanning three days, as the vehicle does not hold a regular stage carriage or contract carriage permit for that route.
what_it_covers: A permit issued under section 87 to authorise a transport vehicle to operate for a short, defined period for a specific purpose such as a pilgrimage, fair, or emergency.
Permits granted to supplement existing transport services during peak demand periods, such as festivals, harvests, or public events, where regular permit capacity is inadequate.
Authorisation for a vehicle not holding a regular permit to operate temporarily on a route or in an area for which the full permit application process has not been completed.
Situations where a transport authority urgently needs to increase vehicle availability without waiting for the ordinary permit-granting procedure under sections 71 or 74.
what_it_excludes: Regular permits issued under sections 72, 74, 76, or 79, which have a standard five-year duration and are subject to the full renewal process under section 81.
Special permits issued under sub-section (8) of section 88, which constitute a distinct category of permit separate from temporary permits under section 87.
National permits or countersigned permits that are subject to their own validity and synchronisation rules under section 88(1) and cannot be classified as temporary permits.
Variations or extensions to existing regular permits under section 80, which are treated as applications for new regular permits and not as temporary permits.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a permit qualifies as a temporary permit under section 87 determines whether it is exempt from the mandatory five-year duration and the structured renewal process under section 81, meaning its expiry, validity, and legal authorisation to ply are governed by entirely different rules. Operating a transport vehicle after a temporary permit's expiry without a valid regular permit constitutes an offence under the Act, exposing the operator to penalty, while the shorter duration also means the permit cannot be treated as conferring any long-term vested right to operate on a route.
